Atomistic modelling of electronic materials under nonequilibrium conditions

发表于2026-08-13|更新于2026-10-01|NUS semester 1
|总字数:21k

Electronic states and atomic arrangements determine a material's structure, reactions and transport. These six chapters start from the electronic ground state: use DFT to calculate energies, derive forces to follow atomic motion, and search the potential energy surface for reaction pathways and barriers.

Chapter Central question
I. Overview How do equilibrium, steady state and nonequilibrium differ? How do electrons and atoms jointly determine material behaviour?
II. DFT and Kohn–Sham Approach How does electron density determine the ground-state energy, and why is self-consistency necessary?
III. Periodic Systems and Pseudopotential How does crystal periodicity simplify electronic structure calculations, and how can their cost be reduced?
IV. Structural Phase Changes How do electronic energies determine atomic forces, motion and structural changes?
V. Thermal Catalysis How do catalysts activate molecules, alter pathways and lower reaction barriers?
VI. Nudged Elastic Band Method How are minimum energy paths and transition states located?

I. Overview

Atomistic modelling starts from atomic nuclei and electrons to explain material structures, reactions, and transport. The electron distribution determines the forces on atoms, while atomic positions determine electronic orbitals and energy levels. Understanding how a material changes therefore usually requires connecting its electronic structure to atomic motion.

The first six chapters establish methods for equilibrium electronic structure calculations, then use total energies and forces to study atomic motion, catalysis, and reaction pathways. Two concrete questions illustrate this approach: why do metal clusters become more active for nitrogen reduction when supported on graphene, and why can small atomic displacements in a molecular junction cause a sudden increase in current?

1. Equilibrium, steady state, and nonequilibrium

A steady state has time-independent macroscopic averages:

d⟨A⟩dt=0.\frac{d\langle A\rangle}{dt}=0. dtd⟨A⟩​=0.

Equilibrium additionally requires the absence of sustained net transport driven by thermodynamic imbalances such as temperature or chemical-potential differences. Connected regions in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature; regions that can exchange the same particle species have the same chemical potential at equilibrium. For charged particles, the transport driving force is described by the electrochemical potential, which includes the effect of the electric potential.

Constant averages do not mean stationary microscopic particles. Particles in an equilibrium gas still move and collide, and their energy distribution depends on momentum. What remains stationary is the statistical distribution. Equilibrium does not imply zero particle momentum or a momentum-independent probability distribution.

Nonequilibrium processes commonly take two forms:

  • Time-dependent processes: atomic positions, electronic states, or other averages change with time, as in structural phase transitions, chemical reactions, electronic excitations, and motion under external forces.
  • Steady-state transport: the system maintains a steady average density while sustaining mass, charge, spin, or heat transport.

A wire connected to a battery is a nonequilibrium steady state. Electrons continuously pass through it, but equal inflow and outflow rates can keep the local average electron number constant. Similarly, water can flow continuously through a pipe while the amount of water inside stays constant. The initial establishment of current is a transient process; a stable current is a steady state. If the current then displaces contact atoms, the structure begins another time-dependent process.

Both an equilibrium gas in a heat bath and a wire carrying a stable current are therefore steady states, but only the former is also in equilibrium.

2. Statistical ensembles: what can the system exchange with its surroundings?

An ensemble is a collection of microstates and their probabilities under specified macroscopic conditions. To choose an ensemble, first determine whether the system can exchange energy, particles, or neither with its surroundings.

Ensemble Fixed macroscopic quantities Exchange with surroundings
Microcanonical N,V,EN,V,EN,V,E Isolated; no energy or particle exchange
Canonical N,V,TN,V,TN,V,T Energy exchange with a heat bath
Grand canonical μ,V,T\mu,V,Tμ,V,T Energy and particle exchange with a reservoir

Microcanonical ensemble

An isolated system has fixed particle number NNN, volume VVV, and energy EEE. If WWW microstates are accessible, they have equal probabilities:

pi=1W,∑i=1Wpi=1.p_i=\frac{1}{W},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{W}p_i=1. pi​=W1​,i=1∑W​pi​=1.

Canonical ensemble

A system in contact with a heat bath has fixed N,V,TN,V,TN,V,T, but its energy can fluctuate. A microstate of energy EiE_iEi​ is weighted by the Boltzmann factor:

pi=e−βEiZ=eβ(F−Ei),β=1kBT.p_i=\frac{e^{-\beta E_i}}{Z} =e^{\beta(F-E_i)},\qquad \beta=\frac{1}{k_{\mathrm B}T}. pi​=Ze−βEi​​=eβ(F−Ei​),β=kB​T1​.

The partition function normalizes the probabilities and determines the Helmholtz free energy:

Z=∑ie−βEi,F=−kBTln⁡Z.Z=\sum_i e^{-\beta E_i},\qquad F=-k_{\mathrm B}T\ln Z. Z=i∑​e−βEi​,F=−kB​TlnZ.

The probability of an individual microstate differs from the total probability of an energy level. If a level EEE has degeneracy g(E)g(E)g(E), its total probability is proportional to g(E)e−βEg(E)e^{-\beta E}g(E)e−βE. Higher energy reduces the weight of each state, whereas greater degeneracy increases the number of states at that energy.

For example, if two nondegenerate states differ in energy by 2kBT2k_{\mathrm B}T2kB​T, the ratio of the higher-state probability to the lower-state probability is e−2≈0.135e^{-2}\approx0.135e−2≈0.135. If these are the only two states, the probability of occupying the higher state is

phigh=e−21+e−2≈0.119.p_{\mathrm{high}}=\frac{e^{-2}}{1+e^{-2}}\approx0.119. phigh​=1+e−2e−2​≈0.119.

Grand canonical ensemble

When a system exchanges both energy and particles with a reservoir, its chemical potential μ\muμ, volume VVV, and temperature TTT are fixed, while its particle number NNN can fluctuate. The statistical weight is determined by E−μNE-\mu NE−μN:

pi,N=e−β(Ei,N−μN)Ξ=eβ(Ω+μN−Ei,N).p_{i,N} =\frac{e^{-\beta(E_{i,N}-\mu N)}}{\Xi} =e^{\beta(\Omega+\mu N-E_{i,N})}. pi,N​=Ξe−β(Ei,N​−μN)​=eβ(Ω+μN−Ei,N​).

The grand partition function and grand potential are

Ξ=∑N∑ie−β(Ei,N−μN),Ω=−kBTln⁡Ξ.\Xi=\sum_N\sum_i e^{-\beta(E_{i,N}-\mu N)},\qquad \Omega=-k_{\mathrm B}T\ln\Xi. Ξ=N∑​i∑​e−β(Ei,N​−μN),Ω=−kB​TlnΞ.

All three ensembles calculate averages by weighting physical quantities with their probabilities:

⟨A⟩=∑ipiAi,\langle A\rangle=\sum_i p_i A_i, ⟨A⟩=i∑​pi​Ai​,

The grand canonical ensemble also requires a sum over particle number. These probabilities describe equilibrium statistics; electrons carrying a steady current generally cannot be described by a single equilibrium distribution shared throughout the system.

3. Coupling between electrons and atoms

Electronic materials consist of ions and electrons. Atomic motion changes electronic orbitals and energy levels; electronic redistribution changes interatomic forces. Bond formation and bond breaking therefore involve both electronic rearrangement and atomic motion.

Time-dependent ion motions include structural phase transitions and chemical reactions. Time-dependent electronic properties include electronic excitations and electronic phase transitions. DC electric currents and spin currents describe steady charge and spin transport. Thermoelectric effects connect electrical and thermal transport, as when a temperature difference produces a voltage.

In many problems involving atomic motion, electrons adjust faster than atoms move. One can first determine the electronic state at fixed atomic positions, then differentiate its energy with respect to those positions to obtain forces and follow the structural evolution. Equilibrium electronic ground-state calculations are thus the starting point for potential energy surfaces, molecular dynamics, and reaction-path calculations.

4. Why do metal clusters on graphene activate nitrogen more readily?

The key is that defective graphene and a partially deligated cluster jointly form a nitrogen-activation site. The metal and a defect C atom bind opposite ends of the nitrogen molecule, while metal electrons enter its π∗\pi^*π∗ antibonding orbitals, weakening the N–N bond and facilitating subsequent hydrogenation. This mechanism explains the Au–Pt and Au–Pd cluster catalysts studied by Yao et al. (2020).

From a ligand-protected cluster to a nitrogen adsorption site

The intact Au4Pt2(SR)8\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{Pt}_2(\mathrm{SR})_8Au4​Pt2​(SR)8​ cluster is surrounded by eight sulfur-containing ligands. During anchoring, two SR\mathrm{SR}SR ligands at the bottom are removed. The exposed Pt bonds to C atoms at the graphene defect edge, anchoring Au4Pt2(SR)6\mathrm{Au}_4\mathrm{Pt}_2(\mathrm{SR})_6Au4​Pt2​(SR)6​ at a divacancy: a defect formed by two missing adjacent C atoms.

Ligand removal also changes the electronic states available for bonding. The energy gap decreases, and singly occupied states derived from Pt 5d5d5d and Au 6s6s6s appear. Each contains one electron and lies at relatively high energy, making electron donation to nitrogen easier. The same cluster on defect-free graphene still cannot adsorb N2\mathrm N_2N2​, showing that ligand removal and the defect site must act together.

Adsorbed nitrogen bridges the cluster and the defect C atom. One end forms a C–N bond, while the other forms a metal–N bond with nearby Pt/Au. This two-ended geometry both holds the molecule in place and brings it into contact with C and metal orbitals that can participate in bonding. The proposed local Pt coordination was also assessed by comparing the main peak positions and shapes of simulated and experimental XANES spectra.

The defect C atom and nearby metal bind opposite ends of nitrogen. Charge-density-difference isosurfaces show electron accumulation and depletion after adsorption; blue atoms mark the nitrogen molecule. The XANES comparison tests the model of local Pt coordination.

Donation, back-donation, and weakening of the N–N bond

After adsorption, nitrogen orbitals mix with metal ddd orbitals. Electron transfer occurs in both directions: occupied nitrogen σ\sigmaσ orbitals donate to the metal, and the metal back-donates into nitrogen π∗\pi^*π∗ orbitals. Back-donation increases antibonding occupation and weakens the N–N bond. The system's Fermi level and nitrogen LUMO differ by approximately 0.6 eV0.6\,\mathrm{eV}0.6eV; Bader analysis gives a net gain of about 1.441.441.44 electrons by nitrogen.

The charge-density difference shows where electrons accumulate or are depleted after adsorption:

Δρ(r)=ρcat+N2(r)−ρcat(r)−ρN2(r).\Delta\rho(\mathbf r) =\rho_{\mathrm{cat}+\mathrm N_2}(\mathbf r) -\rho_{\mathrm{cat}}(\mathbf r) -\rho_{\mathrm N_2}(\mathbf r). Δρ(r)=ρcat+N2​​(r)−ρcat​(r)−ρN2​​(r).

All three densities use the same atomic positions as in the adsorbed geometry. Δρ>0\Delta\rho>0Δρ>0 indicates electron accumulation, and Δρ<0\Delta\rho<0Δρ<0 indicates depletion. Integration over selected regions or charge partitioning can further estimate transferred electron numbers. This comparison describes electronic rearrangement in the system containing adsorbed nitrogen.

The adsorption energy is defined as

Eads=Ecat+N2−Ecat−EN2.E_{\mathrm{ads}} =E_{\mathrm{cat}+\mathrm N_2}-E_{\mathrm{cat}}-E_{\mathrm N_2}. Eads​=Ecat+N2​​−Ecat​−EN2​​.

Here, Eads=−0.38 eVE_{\mathrm{ads}}=-0.38\,\mathrm{eV}Eads​=−0.38eV, so adsorption lowers the energy. Activation does not immediately remove the N–N bond: its occupation and bond strength change first, and successive hydrogenation then converts the two N atoms into ammonia.

Successive hydrogenation, desorption, and energy barriers

The net reaction in an acidic electrolyte is

N2+6H++6e−⟶2NH3.\mathrm N_2+6\mathrm H^++6e^-\longrightarrow2\mathrm{NH}_3. N2​+6H++6e−⟶2NH3​.

It has the same overall atomic stoichiometry as N2+3H2→2NH3\mathrm N_2+3\mathrm H_2\to2\mathrm{NH}_3N2​+3H2​→2NH3​, but the electrochemical reduction is supplied jointly by protons and electrons.

This pathway first hydrogenates the N atom attached to graphene. Three H atoms are added successively, and the first ammonia molecule is released. Another three H atoms are then added to the N still attached to the metal, releasing the second ammonia molecule. Product desorption frees the site for another catalytic cycle. The final ammonia desorption requires about 0.91 eV0.91\,\mathrm{eV}0.91eV, the largest energy cost along this pathway.

The horizontal axis orders the reaction steps, and the vertical axis gives relative energy. The atomic structures show two successive sequences of hydrogenation and ammonia desorption. Values beside the plateaus are energy changes between consecutive steps; intermediate-state energies and transition-state barriers are different quantities.

When reading reaction energies, distinguish the change between consecutive steps from the energy relative to a common starting point. For example, if adsorption lowers the energy by 0.38 eV0.38\,\mathrm{eV}0.38eV and the next step lowers it by another 3.76 eV3.76\,\mathrm{eV}3.76eV, the second plateau lies at −4.14 eV-4.14\,\mathrm{eV}−4.14eV relative to the starting point. Comparing states with different numbers of added H atoms also requires including the reference energy of the added hydrogen.

Reaction energy compares the initial and final states. The activation barrier is measured from the preceding energy minimum to the transition state for that step:

ΔE=Efinal−Einitial,Ea=ETS−Einitial.\Delta E=E_{\mathrm{final}}-E_{\mathrm{initial}},\qquad E_a=E_{\mathrm{TS}}-E_{\mathrm{initial}}. ΔE=Efinal​−Einitial​,Ea​=ETS​−Einitial​.

Intermediate-state energies describe the energetic favourability of a reaction, but its rate also depends on the difficulty of reaching the transition state. Even an exothermic step may first have to cross a high barrier.

Production rate and Faradaic efficiency

The experimental comparison uses potentials relative to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), with ammonia production rates normalized by catalyst mass and time. At −0.1 V-0.1\,\mathrm V−0.1V, graphene-supported Pt clusters produce ammonia at approximately three times the rate of unsupported clusters; the Pd system reaches its peak at −0.2 V-0.2\,\mathrm V−0.2V.

More negative potentials also promote the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). The Pd system suppresses HER more effectively, allowing a higher ammonia production rate at a more negative potential. Optimizing the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) therefore requires both promoting nitrogen activation and hydrogenation and reducing the fraction of electrons consumed by hydrogen evolution.

Faradaic efficiency measures the fraction of total charge used to produce ammonia:

FENH3=3FnNH3Q.\mathrm{FE}_{\mathrm{NH}_3} =\frac{3F n_{\mathrm{NH}_3}}{Q}. FENH3​​=Q3FnNH3​​​.

FFF is the Faraday constant, nNH3n_{\mathrm{NH}_3}nNH3​​ is the amount of ammonia produced in moles, and QQQ is the total charge passed. The factor 3 follows from the three electrons required per ammonia molecule. Production rate describes how quickly ammonia is made; FE describes how efficiently electrons are used for that purpose. If the current doubles while the ammonia production rate stays fixed, QQQ doubles over the same time interval and FE halves.

5. How does bias change the structure and current of a molecular junction?

Bias changes the electron distribution in a molecular junction and therefore changes the forces on its atoms. A structure stable at zero bias may adopt a different configuration when current flows. Wang et al. (2024) studied an oligophenylene-bridged bis-triarylamines junction connected to Au electrodes through S at both ends. The molecule contains five phenyl-ring groups and terminal methyl groups.

The simulations were performed at 300 K300\,\mathrm K300K, allowing the molecule and contact Au atoms to move, with a time step of 2 fs2\,\mathrm{fs}2fs. At 1.4 V1.4\,\mathrm V1.4V, a structural change near the source contact occurred after approximately 100 fs100\,\mathrm{fs}100fs, increasing the average Au–S bond length by about 0.3 A˚0.3\,\text{\AA}0.3A˚. At 1.3 V1.3\,\mathrm V1.3V, the junction continued to fluctuate around its original configuration.

Bias-dependent energy and atomic forces

The effective energy used in this steady-state density functional theory (SS-DFT) calculation contains a bias-dependent term:

E~=ESS+En,En=−eVb2∫ρn(r) d3r.\widetilde E=E_{\mathrm{SS}}+E_n,\qquad E_n=-\frac{eV_b}{2}\int\rho_n(\mathbf r)\,d^3r. E=ESS​+En​,En​=−2eVb​​∫ρn​(r)d3r.

VbV_bVb​ is the bias, e>0e>0e>0 is the elementary charge, and ρn\rho_nρn​ is the nonequilibrium electron density. Atomic forces are the negative derivatives of the full effective energy with respect to atomic positions:

FI=−∂E~∂RI=−∂ESS∂RI−∂En∂RI.\mathbf F_I =-\frac{\partial\widetilde E}{\partial\mathbf R_I} =-\frac{\partial E_{\mathrm{SS}}}{\partial\mathbf R_I} -\frac{\partial E_n}{\partial\mathbf R_I}. FI​=−∂RI​∂E​=−∂RI​∂ESS​​−∂RI​∂En​​.

After the structural change, EnE_nEn​ decreases enough to compensate for an increase in ESSE_{\mathrm{SS}}ESS​. Electronic effects under bias drive the change while the thermostat maintains 300 K300\,\mathrm K300K. The relative effective energies are referenced to the initial configuration at 1.4 V1.4\,\mathrm V1.4V.

This treatment combines an electronic steady state with time-dependent atomic motion. At each instantaneous geometry, the electrons first establish a steady state; the atoms then move more slowly under the corresponding forces. The two timescales describe different degrees of freedom.

From orbital coupling to transmission and current

In fixed-geometry TranSIESTA and SS-DFT calculations, current increases gradually with bias. SS-DFT calculations that allow structural change instead show a sudden current increase near 1.4 V1.4\,\mathrm V1.4V. Atomic displacements and group rotations change the overlap between Au 5d5d5d and S 3p3p3p orbitals at the source contact, producing additional transmission peaks within the bias window.

For coherent transport, the Landauer formula relates the transmission spectrum to current:

I(V)=2eh∫T(E,V)[fL(E)−fR(E)]dE.I(V)=\frac{2e}{h}\int T(E,V)\left[f_L(E)-f_R(E)\right]dE. I(V)=h2e​∫T(E,V)[fL​(E)−fR​(E)]dE.

T(E,V)T(E,V)T(E,V) is the transmission function, fL,fRf_L,f_RfL​,fR​ are the Fermi distributions of the left and right electrodes, and the factor 2 accounts for spin degeneracy. At low temperature, the occupation difference is largest within the bias window between the electrode electrochemical potentials. Transmission changes contribute substantially to net current when they fall within the effective transport window: peaks that grow, broaden, or move into the window can all increase the integral.

Orbital overlap depends on distance, orientation, and symmetry. Group rotation can improve the coupling of relevant orbitals even as the Au–S bond lengthens, so bond length alone does not determine current. The full transmission spectrum determines the Landauer integral. At fixed bias, if T(E,V)T(E,V)T(E,V) doubles throughout the window while electrode distributions remain unchanged, the current doubles too.

6. Learning goals and checks

Understanding atomistic modelling means being able to identify the degrees of freedom being calculated, the approximations used, the inputs and outputs, and how the results explain material behaviour. The first six chapters cover equilibrium electronic structure, periodic systems, atomic motion, thermal catalysis, and reaction pathways. Necessary formulas are provided in the closed-book test, so revision should focus on notation, applicability, calculation steps, and physical meaning.

Use these three questions to check the main ideas:

  1. Are time-independent macroscopic averages sufficient to establish equilibrium? No. Check whether temperature or electrochemical-potential differences sustain net transport.
  2. Why does graphene enhance activity in the nitrogen reduction system? Defect C and the partially deligated cluster jointly bind nitrogen. Ligand removal creates relatively high-energy occupied states, allowing metal-to-nitrogen π∗\pi^*π∗ back-donation that weakens the N–N bond for subsequent hydrogenation.
  3. If the initial, transition, and final states have energies 000, 0.600.600.60, and −0.40 eV-0.40\,\mathrm{eV}−0.40eV, what are the reaction energy and forward and reverse barriers? They are −0.40-0.40−0.40, 0.600.600.60, and 1.00 eV1.00\,\mathrm{eV}1.00eV, respectively. The reaction is exothermic but still has a forward barrier.

II. Equilibrium Modelling: Density Functional Theory and Kohn–Sham Approach

Given the atomic species and positions, electron number, and external conditions, the first task is to calculate the electronic ground-state density and total energy. Comparing total energies for different atomic arrangements reveals their relative stability. Studying how energy changes with atomic positions then gives forces and potential energy surfaces.

Density functional theory (DFT) uses the electron density as its basic variable. The Hohenberg–Kohn theorems explain why density is sufficient to describe the ground state; the Kohn–Sham method provides solvable auxiliary orbital equations; and LDA, GGA, and LSDA approximate the exchange-correlation functional required in practical calculations.

1. From the many-electron wavefunction to electron density

The many-electron problem begins with the Schrödinger equation:

H^Ψ=EΨ,⟨A⟩=⟨Ψ∣A^∣Ψ⟩.\hat H\Psi=E\Psi,\qquad \langle A\rangle=\langle\Psi|\hat A|\Psi\rangle. H^Ψ=EΨ,⟨A⟩=⟨Ψ∣A^∣Ψ⟩.

With nuclear positions fixed, the electronic Hamiltonian is

H^=−ℏ22me∑i∇i2−∑i,IZIe24πϵ0riI+∑i<je24πϵ0rij.\hat H =-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\sum_i\nabla_i^2 -\sum_{i,I}\frac{Z_Ie^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r_{iI}} +\sum_{i<j}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r_{ij}}. H^=−2me​ℏ2​i∑​∇i2​−i,I∑​4πϵ0​riI​ZI​e2​+i<j∑​4πϵ0​rij​e2​.

The three terms are electron kinetic energy, electron–nucleus attraction, and electron–electron repulsion. i,ji,ji,j label electrons, III labels nuclei, ZIZ_IZI​ is the nuclear charge number, and i<ji<ji<j ensures that each electron pair is counted once. Nuclear repulsion is constant during the electronic solution at fixed nuclear positions; it must be added back when comparing total energies of different structures.

A wavefunction for NNN electrons depends on 3N3N3N spatial coordinates as well as spin. The electron density ρ(r)\rho(\mathbf r)ρ(r) depends only on a three-dimensional position and satisfies

ρ(r)≥0,∫ρ(r) d3r=N.\rho(\mathbf r)\ge0,\qquad \int\rho(\mathbf r)\,d^3r=N. ρ(r)≥0,∫ρ(r)d3r=N.

The true many-electron density is obtained by integrating over the other electrons' coordinates and summing over spin:

ρ(r)=N∑σ1∫∣Ψ(rσ1,x2,…,xN)∣2 dx2⋯dxN.\rho(\mathbf r) =N\sum_{\sigma_1}\int \left|\Psi(\mathbf r\sigma_1,x_2,\ldots,x_N)\right|^2 \,dx_2\cdots dx_N. ρ(r)=Nσ1​∑​∫∣Ψ(rσ1​,x2​,…,xN​)∣2dx2​⋯dxN​.

xjx_jxj​ includes the position and spin of electron jjj, and dxjdx_jdxj​ includes the corresponding integration and summation. Density describes the average number of electrons near a point; it is not obtained by treating the many-electron wavefunction as a single three-dimensional function and simply taking its squared modulus.

The first Hohenberg–Kohn theorem

For a fixed electron–electron interaction, the ground-state density determines the external potential Vext(r)V_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r)Vext​(r) up to an additive constant. It therefore determines the Hamiltonian and ground-state properties. Adding a constant to the external potential only shifts the energy zero.

Ground-state observables can be written as functionals of the density:

⟨A⟩=A[ρ].\langle A\rangle=A[\rho]. ⟨A⟩=A[ρ].

A functional maps a function to a number: its input is an entire density distribution, and its output is a number. The theorem establishes that density contains sufficient information, but does not supply the explicit energy functional.

The second Hohenberg–Kohn theorem and the variational principle

The electronic energy is written as

E[ρ]=FHK[ρ]+∫ρ(r)Vext(r) d3r,FHK[ρ]=T[ρ]+Vee[ρ].E[\rho]=F_{\mathrm{HK}}[\rho] +\int\rho(\mathbf r)V_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r)\,d^3r, \qquad F_{\mathrm{HK}}[\rho]=T[\rho]+V_{ee}[\rho]. E[ρ]=FHK​[ρ]+∫ρ(r)Vext​(r)d3r,FHK​[ρ]=T[ρ]+Vee​[ρ].

TTT is the true many-electron kinetic energy, and VeeV_{ee}Vee​ is the electron interaction energy. FHKF_{\mathrm{HK}}FHK​ is a universal functional: for a fixed electron interaction, it does not depend on the external potential of a particular material. The atomic configuration enters through VextV_{\mathrm{ext}}Vext​.

At fixed external potential and electron number, the ground-state density minimizes the energy:

E0=min⁡ρ→NE[ρ],E[ρ~]≥E0.E_0=\min_{\rho\to N}E[\rho],\qquad E[\widetilde\rho]\ge E_0. E0​=ρ→Nmin​E[ρ],E[ρ​]≥E0​.

An admissible trial density must be nonnegative, integrate to NNN, and arise from a valid many-electron state. The conventional variational method minimizes ⟨Ψ∣H^∣Ψ⟩\langle\Psi|\hat H|\Psi\rangle⟨Ψ∣H^∣Ψ⟩ over normalized wavefunctions, whereas DFT minimizes E[ρ]E[\rho]E[ρ] over admissible densities. Both seek the same ground state.

This comparison concerns different trial densities evaluated with the same exact functional. If two approximate functionals give −10-10−10 and −11 eV-11\,\mathrm{eV}−11eV, the lower value alone does not establish greater accuracy.

2. Hartree energy and the Kohn–Sham auxiliary system

From this point onward, atomic units are used: ℏ=me=e=4πϵ0=1\hbar=m_e=e=4\pi\epsilon_0=1ℏ=me​=e=4πϵ0​=1. The external-potential energy can be evaluated directly by integrating the density. The classical part of the electron–electron interaction is the Hartree energy:

EH[ρ]=J[ρ]=12∬ρ(r)ρ(r′)∣r−r′∣ d3r d3r′.E_H[\rho]=J[\rho] =\frac12\iint \frac{\rho(\mathbf r)\rho(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|} \,d^3r\,d^3r'. EH​[ρ]=J[ρ]=21​∬∣r−r′∣ρ(r)ρ(r′)​d3rd3r′.

It treats electrons as a continuous charge cloud. The double integral counts both (r,r′)(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')(r,r′) and (r′,r)(\mathbf r',\mathbf r)(r′,r), so the factor 1/21/21/2 avoids double counting.

The Hartree mean field does not fully include exchange and correlation. Exchange arises from the antisymmetry of a fermionic wavefunction; correlation describes correlated electron motion beyond an independent-particle approximation. The true kinetic energy T[ρ]T[\rho]T[ρ] is also difficult to express directly as a simple density functional.

Calculating kinetic energy from auxiliary orbitals

The Kohn–Sham method constructs an auxiliary system of noninteracting electrons with the same ground-state density as the real system. Its wavefunction can be represented by a Slater determinant:

Φs=1N!det⁡[φi(xj)].\Phi_s=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\det[\varphi_i(x_j)]. Φs​=N!​1​det[φi​(xj​)].

Exchanging two electrons changes the determinant's sign, automatically satisfying the Pauli principle. Each occupied spin orbital holds at most one electron. With fif_ifi​ denoting the occupation number, the density and auxiliary kinetic energy are

ρ(r)=∑ifi∣φi(r)∣2,Ts=∑ifi⟨φi∣−12∇2∣φi⟩.\rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_i f_i|\varphi_i(\mathbf r)|^2, \qquad T_s=\sum_i f_i \left\langle\varphi_i\left|-\frac12\nabla^2\right|\varphi_i\right\rangle. ρ(r)=i∑​fi​∣φi​(r)∣2,Ts​=i∑​fi​⟨φi​∣∣∣∣∣​−21​∇2∣∣∣∣∣​φi​⟩.

For spin-degenerate spatial orbitals, double occupation corresponds to fi=2f_i=2fi​=2; for separately represented spin orbitals, occupation cannot exceed 1. The true wavefunction and auxiliary Slater determinant may differ, but their electron densities must agree.

The exact exchange-correlation decomposition

The Kohn–Sham total energy is written as

E[ρ]=Ts[ρ]+∫ρVext d3r+EH[ρ]+Exc[ρ],E[\rho]=T_s[\rho] +\int\rho V_{\mathrm{ext}}\,d^3r +E_H[\rho]+E_{\mathrm{xc}}[\rho], E[ρ]=Ts​[ρ]+∫ρVext​d3r+EH​[ρ]+Exc​[ρ],

where

Exc[ρ]=(T[ρ]−Ts[ρ])+(Vee[ρ]−EH[ρ]).E_{\mathrm{xc}}[\rho] =\bigl(T[\rho]-T_s[\rho]\bigr) +\bigl(V_{ee}[\rho]-E_H[\rho]\bigr). Exc​[ρ]=(T[ρ]−Ts​[ρ])+(Vee​[ρ]−EH​[ρ]).

Thus, TsT_sTs​ is not equal to the true kinetic energy TTT. The kinetic-energy difference T−TsT-T_sT−Ts​ is included in ExcE_{\mathrm{xc}}Exc​ together with the nonclassical interaction energy. Given the exact ExcE_{\mathrm{xc}}Exc​, this decomposition is itself exact. Practical calculations usually introduce an approximation when selecting the exchange-correlation functional.

For example, if T=12,Ts=10,Vee=8,EH=9T=12,T_s=10,V_{ee}=8,E_H=9T=12,Ts​=10,Vee​=8,EH​=9 in consistent energy units, then Exc=(12−10)+(8−9)=1E_{\mathrm{xc}}=(12-10)+(8-9)=1Exc​=(12−10)+(8−9)=1. Calculating only Vee−EH=−1V_{ee}-E_H=-1Vee​−EH​=−1 would omit the kinetic-energy difference.

3. Deriving the Kohn–Sham equations variationally

The auxiliary orbitals satisfy orthonormality:

∫φi∗(r)φj(r) d3r=δij.\int\varphi_i^*(\mathbf r)\varphi_j(\mathbf r)\,d^3r=\delta_{ij}. ∫φi∗​(r)φj​(r)d3r=δij​.

Each orbital is normalized, and distinct orbitals are orthogonal. The complex conjugate must be retained for general complex orbitals. For this derivation, take the occupation of each occupied spin orbital to be 1 and impose these conditions using Lagrange multipliers:

L=E−∑ijϵij(∫φi∗φj d3r−δij),δLδφi∗=0.\mathcal L =E-\sum_{ij}\epsilon_{ij} \left(\int\varphi_i^*\varphi_j\,d^3r-\delta_{ij}\right), \qquad \frac{\delta\mathcal L}{\delta\varphi_i^*}=0. L=E−ij∑​ϵij​(∫φi∗​φj​d3r−δij​),δφi∗​δL​=0.

Variation of the kinetic energy with respect to an orbital gives −12∇2φi-\tfrac12\nabla^2\varphi_i−21​∇2φi​; the density dependence of the remaining energy terms produces the effective potential. Diagonalizing the multiplier matrix ϵij\epsilon_{ij}ϵij​ gives the Kohn–Sham equation in single-electron form:

[−12∇2+Veff(r)]φi(r)=ϵiφi(r),\left[-\frac12\nabla^2+V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf r)\right] \varphi_i(\mathbf r)=\epsilon_i\varphi_i(\mathbf r), [−21​∇2+Veff​(r)]φi​(r)=ϵi​φi​(r),

Veff=Vext+VH+Vxc,V_{\mathrm{eff}}=V_{\mathrm{ext}}+V_H+V_{\mathrm{xc}}, Veff​=Vext​+VH​+Vxc​,

VH(r)=∫ρ(r′)∣r−r′∣ d3r′,Vxc(r)=δExcδρ(r).V_H(\mathbf r) =\int\frac{\rho(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d^3r', \qquad V_{\mathrm{xc}}(\mathbf r) =\frac{\delta E_{\mathrm{xc}}}{\delta\rho(\mathbf r)}. VH​(r)=∫∣r−r′∣ρ(r′)​d3r′,Vxc​(r)=δρ(r)δExc​​.

The Hartree potential has no factor 1/21/21/2: varying EHE_HEH​ produces one contribution from each density factor, cancelling that coefficient. The meaning of a functional derivative can be expressed as

δExc=∫Vxc(r) δρ(r) d3r,\delta E_{\mathrm{xc}} =\int V_{\mathrm{xc}}(\mathbf r)\,\delta\rho(\mathbf r)\,d^3r, δExc​=∫Vxc​(r)δρ(r)d3r,

which gives the first-order exchange-correlation energy change caused by a small density variation.

Although these equations have a single-electron form, the effective potential still depends on the total density produced by all occupied orbitals. The total energy also includes corrections to the counting of interactions, so it cannot simply be replaced by the eigenvalue sum ∑ifiϵi\sum_i f_i\epsilon_i∑i​fi​ϵi​.

4. Self-consistent field: matching the input and output densities

The Kohn–Sham solution is circular: density determines the potential, the potential determines the orbitals, and the orbitals produce a new density. A self-consistent field (SCF) calculation proceeds as follows:

  1. Choose an initial density that integrates to NNN, denoted by ρin\rho_{\mathrm{in}}ρin​.
  2. Use it to construct VHV_HVH​ and VxcV_{\mathrm{xc}}Vxc​, then combine them with the known external potential to obtain VeffV_{\mathrm{eff}}Veff​.
  3. Solve the Kohn–Sham eigenvalue equations and determine orbital occupations from the electron number.
  4. Calculate ρout=∑ifi∣φi∣2\rho_{\mathrm{out}}=\sum_i f_i|\varphi_i|^2ρout​=∑i​fi​∣φi​∣2 from the orbitals.
  5. Compare the input and output densities and check the energy change. If convergence has not been reached, update the input and repeat.

The self-consistency condition is

ρout[ρin]=ρin.\rho_{\mathrm{out}}[\rho_{\mathrm{in}}]=\rho_{\mathrm{in}}. ρout​[ρin​]=ρin​.

A single eigenvalue solution only gives orbitals in the current potential. Self-consistency requires the density produced by those orbitals to match the density used to construct that potential. Numerically, the density difference and energy change must fall below specified tolerances.

Replacing the input entirely with the new density can cause oscillations. Simple density mixing combines the old and new densities:

ρin(n+1)=(1−α)ρin(n)+αρout(n),0<α≤1.\rho_{\mathrm{in}}^{(n+1)} =(1-\alpha)\rho_{\mathrm{in}}^{(n)} +\alpha\rho_{\mathrm{out}}^{(n)}, \qquad 0<\alpha\le1. ρin(n+1)​=(1−α)ρin(n)​+αρout(n)​,0<α≤1.

A smaller α\alphaα gives a more conservative update. For example, if the input and output densities at a point are 0.800.800.80 and 1.201.201.20, with α=0.25\alpha=0.25α=0.25, the next input is 0.75×0.80+0.25×1.20=0.900.75\times0.80+0.25\times1.20=0.900.75×0.80+0.25×1.20=0.90. If both density distributions integrate to NNN, their mixture preserves the total electron number.

5. LDA: using a uniform electron gas locally

The local density approximation (LDA) estimates the exchange-correlation energy per electron at each point using a uniform electron gas of the same density, then multiplies by the local density and integrates over space:

ExcLDA[ρ]=∫ρ(r) ϵxc(ρ(r)) d3r.E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{LDA}}[\rho] =\int\rho(\mathbf r)\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho(\mathbf r))\,d^3r. ExcLDA​[ρ]=∫ρ(r)ϵxc​(ρ(r))d3r.

ϵxc\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}ϵxc​ is an energy per electron, whereas ρϵxc\rho\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}ρϵxc​ is an energy per unit volume. The material's density may still vary spatially; "local" means that the energy at each point uses only the density value at that point.

Because the density dependence is local, the functional derivative reduces to an ordinary derivative:

VxcLDA=d[ρϵxc(ρ)]dρ=ϵxc+ρdϵxcdρ.V_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{LDA}} =\frac{d[\rho\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho)]}{d\rho} =\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}+\rho\frac{d\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}}{d\rho}. VxcLDA​=dρd[ρϵxc​(ρ)]​=ϵxc​+ρdρdϵxc​​.

The first term comes from the density prefactor, and the second from the density dependence of the energy per electron. The potential requires differentiating the whole product. For example,

ϵx=−Cρ1/3⟹Ex=−C∫ρ4/3 d3r,Vx=−4C3ρ1/3.\epsilon_{\mathrm x}=-C\rho^{1/3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_{\mathrm x}=-C\int\rho^{4/3}\,d^3r, \qquad V_{\mathrm x}=-\frac{4C}{3}\rho^{1/3}. ϵx​=−Cρ1/3⟹Ex​=−C∫ρ4/3d3r,Vx​=−34C​ρ1/3.

6. GGA and BLYP: including spatial density variations

Two points can have the same density but different rates of variation in their surroundings. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) also uses the density gradient as an input:

ExcGGA[ρ]=∫ρ(r) ϵxc(ρ,∇ρ) d3r,Exc=Ex+Ec.E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{GGA}}[\rho] =\int\rho(\mathbf r)\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho,\nabla\rho)\,d^3r, \qquad E_{\mathrm{xc}}=E_{\mathrm x}+E_{\mathrm c}. ExcGGA​[ρ]=∫ρ(r)ϵxc​(ρ,∇ρ)d3r,Exc​=Ex​+Ec​.

∇ρ\nabla\rho∇ρ describes the direction and rate of density variation. Exchange and correlation can still be calculated separately and added. BLYP combines Becke exchange with Lee–Yang–Parr correlation; PBE is the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof functional. Changing the functional changes the exchange-correlation energy and potential, while the Kohn–Sham equations and SCF procedure remain the same.

Why does the GGA potential contain a divergence term?

Writing Exc=∫g(ρ,∇ρ) d3rE_{\mathrm{xc}}=\int g(\rho,\nabla\rho)\,d^3rExc​=∫g(ρ,∇ρ)d3r, a variation in density also changes its gradient:

δExc=∫[∂g∂ρ δρ+∂g∂(∇ρ)⋅∇δρ]d3r.\delta E_{\mathrm{xc}} =\int\left[ \frac{\partial g}{\partial\rho}\,\delta\rho +\frac{\partial g}{\partial(\nabla\rho)}\cdot\nabla\delta\rho \right]d^3r. δExc​=∫[∂ρ∂g​δρ+∂(∇ρ)∂g​⋅∇δρ]d3r.

Integrating the second term by parts and taking the boundary term to vanish gives

Vxc=∂g∂ρ−∇⋅∂g∂(∇ρ).V_{\mathrm{xc}} =\frac{\partial g}{\partial\rho} -\nabla\cdot\frac{\partial g}{\partial(\nabla\rho)}. Vxc​=∂ρ∂g​−∇⋅∂(∇ρ)∂g​.

The first term is the contribution from changing the density directly; the second comes from changing its gradient. Differentiating only the explicit ρ\rhoρ dependence would miss the second contribution.

Local exchange, gradient corrections, and correlation in BLYP

Using the dimensionless relative density gradient

x=∣∇ρ∣ρ4/3,x=\frac{|\nabla\rho|}{\rho^{4/3}}, x=ρ4/3∣∇ρ∣​,

the Becke exchange form used in this course is

Ex=−∫Cxρ4/3 d3r−∫bρ4/3x21+6bxarsinh⁡(x) d3r.E_{\mathrm x} =-\int C_{\mathrm x}\rho^{4/3}\,d^3r -\int b\rho^{4/3} \frac{x^2}{1+6bx\operatorname{arsinh}(x)}\,d^3r. Ex​=−∫Cx​ρ4/3d3r−∫bρ4/31+6bxarsinh(x)x2​d3r.

CxC_{\mathrm x}Cx​ and bbb are parameters. The first term is local exchange, and the second is the gradient correction. For a uniform density, ∇ρ=0\nabla\rho=0∇ρ=0, so x=0x=0x=0; the correction vanishes and local exchange is recovered. Here sinh⁡−1(x)\sinh^{-1}(x)sinh−1(x) means the inverse hyperbolic sine, arsinh⁡(x)\operatorname{arsinh}(x)arsinh(x), which differs from 1/sinh⁡(x)1/\sinh(x)1/sinh(x).

LYP correlation uses the density, its derivatives, an auxiliary quantity t(r)t(\mathbf r)t(r), and parameters a,b,c,da,b,c,da,b,c,d to describe correlation in a nonuniform electron distribution. The Laplacian ∇2ρ\nabla^2\rho∇2ρ describes local density curvature. The correlation potential used in self-consistent calculations is still obtained from Vc=δEc/δρV_{\mathrm c}=\delta E_{\mathrm c}/\delta\rhoVc​=δEc​/δρ; correlation energy itself is not a potential.

7. Spin-DFT: solving for both spin channels

Magnetic systems require separate spin-up and spin-down densities. Here the collinear-spin description defines both channels along a common quantization axis.

ρ=ρ↑+ρ↓,ρσ(r)=∑ifiσ∣φiσ(r)∣2,σ=↑,↓.\rho=\rho_\uparrow+\rho_\downarrow,\qquad \rho_\sigma(\mathbf r) =\sum_i f_{i\sigma}|\varphi_{i\sigma}(\mathbf r)|^2, \qquad \sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow. ρ=ρ↑​+ρ↓​,ρσ​(r)=i∑​fiσ​∣φiσ​(r)∣2,σ=↑,↓.

Each channel satisfies

[−12∇2+Veff,σ(r)]φiσ=ϵiσφiσ,\left[-\frac12\nabla^2+V_{\mathrm{eff},\sigma}(\mathbf r)\right] \varphi_{i\sigma} =\epsilon_{i\sigma}\varphi_{i\sigma}, [−21​∇2+Veff,σ​(r)]φiσ​=ϵiσ​φiσ​,

Veff,σ=Vext,σ+VH[ρ↑+ρ↓]+δExc[ρ↑,ρ↓]δρσ.V_{\mathrm{eff},\sigma} =V_{\mathrm{ext},\sigma} +V_H[\rho_\uparrow+\rho_\downarrow] +\frac{\delta E_{\mathrm{xc}}[\rho_\uparrow,\rho_\downarrow]}{\delta\rho_\sigma}. Veff,σ​=Vext,σ​+VH​[ρ↑​+ρ↓​]+δρσ​δExc​[ρ↑​,ρ↓​]​.

Both channels share the Hartree potential generated by the total charge density. The exchange-correlation potentials depend on how electrons are distributed between the spin channels. Updating one channel therefore affects the other through the effective potentials, so both densities must be iterated together.

Electron number, spin imbalance, and Zeeman energy

Define

Nσ=∫ρσ d3r,Mz=μB(N↑−N↓)=μB∫(ρ↑−ρ↓) d3r.N_\sigma=\int\rho_\sigma\,d^3r,\qquad M_z=\mu_{\mathrm B}(N_\uparrow-N_\downarrow) =\mu_{\mathrm B}\int(\rho_\uparrow-\rho_\downarrow)\,d^3r. Nσ​=∫ρσ​d3r,Mz​=μB​(N↑​−N↓​)=μB​∫(ρ↑​−ρ↓​)d3r.

μB\mu_{\mathrm B}μB​ is the Bohr magneton. Here MzM_zMz​ follows the convention based on the difference in spin populations; an electron's physical spin magnetic moment points opposite to its spin. If N↑=6,N↓=4N_\uparrow=6,N_\downarrow=4N↑​=6,N↓​=4, then N=10,Mz=2μBN=10,M_z=2\mu_{\mathrm B}N=10,Mz​=2μB​. If each channel contains 5 electrons, the integrated spin imbalance vanishes, but positive and negative local spin polarizations may still cancel in the integral.

For a magnetic field along zzz, with S^z\hat S_zS^z​ eigenvalues taken as ±1/2\pm1/2±1/2, the Hamiltonian including the Zeeman term is

H^=T^+V^ee+V^ext+2μBB∑iS^zi.\hat H =\hat T+\hat V_{ee}+\hat V_{\mathrm{ext}} +2\mu_{\mathrm B}B\sum_i\hat S_{zi}. H^=T^+V^ee​+V^ext​+2μB​Bi∑​S^zi​.

The single-electron energies in the up and down channels shift by +μBB+\mu_{\mathrm B}B+μB​B and −μBB-\mu_{\mathrm B}B−μB​B, respectively. Their total contribution is +BMz+BM_z+BMz​ under the convention above:

⟨V^extB⟩=∫ρVext d3r+BMz.\langle\hat V_{\mathrm{ext}}^B\rangle =\int\rho V_{\mathrm{ext}}\,d^3r+BM_z. ⟨V^extB​⟩=∫ρVext​d3r+BMz​.

Without a spin-dependent external field, both channels use the same external potential. With a Zeeman term, each channel receives the magnetic-field potential with the appropriate sign.

Energy and self-consistency in a spin-polarized system

The energy is decomposed as

E=Ts[ρ↑,ρ↓]+Eext+EH[ρ]+Exc[ρ↑,ρ↓],E=T_s[\rho_\uparrow,\rho_\downarrow] +E_{\mathrm{ext}}+E_H[\rho] +E_{\mathrm{xc}}[\rho_\uparrow,\rho_\downarrow], E=Ts​[ρ↑​,ρ↓​]+Eext​+EH​[ρ]+Exc​[ρ↑​,ρ↓​],

Ts=∑σ=↑,↓∑ifiσ⟨φiσ∣−12∇2∣φiσ⟩.T_s=\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_i f_{i\sigma} \left\langle\varphi_{i\sigma}\left|-\frac12\nabla^2\right|\varphi_{i\sigma}\right\rangle. Ts​=σ=↑,↓∑​i∑​fiσ​⟨φiσ​∣∣∣∣∣​−21​∇2∣∣∣∣∣​φiσ​⟩.

Hartree energy depends only on total density: two spin distributions with the same total density have the same EHE_HEH​. Kinetic and exchange-correlation energies also depend on spin occupation. Exchange depends on same-spin occupations, and correlation also depends on the spin distribution. ExcE_{\mathrm{xc}}Exc​ retains both spin densities as inputs and includes the difference between the true and auxiliary kinetic energies.

A spin-dependent SCF calculation starts from two initial densities, constructs two potentials, solves for two sets of orbitals, and updates both densities. Convergence must be checked for both charge and spin density: equal and opposite changes in the two channels leave total charge unchanged while changing spin polarization. Different initial magnetizations may converge to different self-consistent magnetic states. To determine the stable state, compare their total energies under the same conditions.

8. LSDA and spin-polarization interpolation

The local spin density approximation (LSDA) uses a uniform electron gas with the same total density and spin distribution at each point:

ExcLSDA[ρ↑,ρ↓]=∫ρ ϵxc(ρ↑,ρ↓) d3r,ρ=ρ↑+ρ↓.E_{\mathrm{xc}}^{\mathrm{LSDA}}[\rho_\uparrow,\rho_\downarrow] =\int\rho\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho_\uparrow,\rho_\downarrow)\,d^3r, \qquad \rho=\rho_\uparrow+\rho_\downarrow. ExcLSDA​[ρ↑​,ρ↓​]=∫ρϵxc​(ρ↑​,ρ↓​)d3r,ρ=ρ↑​+ρ↓​.

Take a functional derivative with respect to each channel separately:

Vxc,↑=ϵxc+ρ∂ϵxc∂ρ↑,Vxc,↓=ϵxc+ρ∂ϵxc∂ρ↓.V_{\mathrm{xc},\uparrow} =\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}} +\rho\frac{\partial\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}}{\partial\rho_\uparrow}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{xc},\downarrow} =\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}} +\rho\frac{\partial\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}}{\partial\rho_\downarrow}. Vxc,↑​=ϵxc​+ρ∂ρ↑​∂ϵxc​​,Vxc,↓​=ϵxc​+ρ∂ρ↓​∂ϵxc​​.

When differentiating with respect to ρ↑\rho_\uparrowρ↑​, hold ρ↓\rho_\downarrowρ↓​ fixed, so ∂ρ/∂ρ↑=1\partial\rho/\partial\rho_\uparrow=1∂ρ/∂ρ↑​=1. Differentiating the total-density prefactor produces the first term; differentiating the energy per electron produces the second. The other spin density is held fixed, while total density changes with the channel being varied. The down-spin derivation is analogous, and the two potentials can differ.

For example, starting from

Ex=−C∫(ρ↑4/3+ρ↓4/3)d3rE_{\mathrm x}=-C\int \left(\rho_\uparrow^{4/3}+\rho_\downarrow^{4/3}\right)d^3r Ex​=−C∫(ρ↑4/3​+ρ↓4/3​)d3r

the up-spin exchange potential is

Vx,↑=−4C3ρ↑1/3.V_{\mathrm x,\uparrow} =-\frac{4C}{3}\rho_\uparrow^{1/3}. Vx,↑​=−34C​ρ↑1/3​.

Representing both channels by total density and spin polarization

Spin polarization is defined as

ξ=ρ↑−ρ↓ρ↑+ρ↓,−1≤ξ≤1.\xi=\frac{\rho_\uparrow-\rho_\downarrow}{\rho_\uparrow+\rho_\downarrow}, \qquad -1\le\xi\le1. ξ=ρ↑​+ρ↓​ρ↑​−ρ↓​​,−1≤ξ≤1.

Hence,

ρ↑=ρ2(1+ξ),ρ↓=ρ2(1−ξ).\rho_\uparrow=\frac{\rho}{2}(1+\xi),\qquad \rho_\downarrow=\frac{\rho}{2}(1-\xi). ρ↑​=2ρ​(1+ξ),ρ↓​=2ρ​(1−ξ).

ξ\xiξ is a local quantity: ξ=0\xi=0ξ=0 means equal spin densities, while ξ=1\xi=1ξ=1 and −1-1−1 represent complete up-spin and down-spin polarization, respectively. At the same total density, one can interpolate between unpolarized and fully polarized uniform electron gases:

ϵxc(ρ,ξ)=ϵxc(ρ,0)+[ϵxc(ρ,1)−ϵxc(ρ,0)]f(ξ),\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho,\xi) =\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho,0) +\left[\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho,1)-\epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho,0)\right]f(\xi), ϵxc​(ρ,ξ)=ϵxc​(ρ,0)+[ϵxc​(ρ,1)−ϵxc​(ρ,0)]f(ξ),

f(ξ)=(1+ξ)4/3+(1−ξ)4/3−224/3−2.f(\xi) =\frac{(1+\xi)^{4/3}+(1-\xi)^{4/3}-2}{2^{4/3}-2}. f(ξ)=24/3−2(1+ξ)4/3+(1−ξ)4/3−2​.

The denominator gives unit weight at full polarization. Interchanging spin-up and spin-down only changes the sign of ξ\xiξ, so

f(0)=0,f(1)=f(−1)=1,f(ξ)=f(−ξ).f(0)=0,\qquad f(1)=f(-1)=1,\qquad f(\xi)=f(-\xi). f(0)=0,f(1)=f(−1)=1,f(ξ)=f(−ξ).

For example, if ρ↑=0.06,ρ↓=0.02\rho_\uparrow=0.06,\rho_\downarrow=0.02ρ↑​=0.06,ρ↓​=0.02, then ρ=0.08,ξ=0.5\rho=0.08,\xi=0.5ρ=0.08,ξ=0.5. If the endpoint exchange-correlation energies per electron at this same total density are −0.50-0.50−0.50 and −0.60-0.60−0.60, then

f(0.5)≈0.219,ϵxc(ρ,0.5)=−0.50−0.10×0.219≈−0.522.f(0.5)\approx0.219,\qquad \epsilon_{\mathrm{xc}}(\rho,0.5) =-0.50-0.10\times0.219\approx-0.522. f(0.5)≈0.219,ϵxc​(ρ,0.5)=−0.50−0.10×0.219≈−0.522.

The interpolation weight is f(ξ)f(\xi)f(ξ), not simply ξ\xiξ.

9. Three questions to answer before calculating

  1. Why is one solution of the Kohn–Sham eigenvalue equations insufficient? The effective potential comes from the input density, while the orbitals generate the output density. Self-consistency requires the two to agree.
  2. Why is ExcE_{\mathrm{xc}}Exc​ more than Vee−EHV_{ee}-E_HVee​−EH​? Once the auxiliary kinetic energy TsT_sTs​ is used, the true kinetic-energy difference T−TsT-T_sT−Ts​ must also be included.
  3. If total charge density has stopped changing, is spin-DFT necessarily converged? No. The two channels may change in opposite directions while preserving total density. Spin density and energy must also be checked.

III. Periodic Systems and Pseudopotential

1. Kohn–Sham calculations for periodic systems

A crystal calculation still begins with the electronic ground state at fixed atomic positions. Hohenberg–Kohn theory expresses this as a variational problem in the density: hold the external potential and electron number fixed, and find the admissible density that minimizes the energy.

E[ρ]=∫Vext(r)ρ(r) dr+FHK[ρ],∫ρ(r) dr=Ne.E[\rho]=\int V_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r)\rho(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r+F_{\mathrm{HK}}[\rho], \qquad \int\rho(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r=N_e. E[ρ]=∫Vext​(r)ρ(r)dr+FHK​[ρ],∫ρ(r)dr=Ne​.

FHKF_{\mathrm{HK}}FHK​ contains the true electronic kinetic energy and electron–electron interactions; the atomic species and arrangement enter through the external potential VextV_{\mathrm{ext}}Vext​. The Kohn–Sham method uses auxiliary one-electron orbitals to calculate the auxiliary system's kinetic energy, placing the remaining contributions in the exchange-correlation functional. In atomic units, the equations are

[−12∇2+Veff(r)]φi(r)=εiφi(r),\left[-\frac12\nabla^2+V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf r)\right]\varphi_i(\mathbf r) =\varepsilon_i\varphi_i(\mathbf r), [−21​∇2+Veff​(r)]φi​(r)=εi​φi​(r),

Veff=Vext+VH+Vxc,ρ(r)=∑ifi∣φi(r)∣2.V_{\mathrm{eff}}=V_{\mathrm{ext}}+V_{\mathrm H}+V_{\mathrm{xc}}, \qquad \rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_i f_i|\varphi_i(\mathbf r)|^2. Veff​=Vext​+VH​+Vxc​,ρ(r)=i∑​fi​∣φi​(r)∣2.

fif_ifi​ is the occupation number. The Hartree potential describes the classical Coulomb interaction of the electron density, while the exchange-correlation potential accounts for quantum effects missing from this mean-field description. The potential depends on the density, and the occupied orbitals of that potential produce the density. A self-consistent calculation is therefore required: guess the density, construct the potential, solve for the orbitals, and update the density until input and output agree.

εi\varepsilon_iεi​ is an auxiliary orbital eigenvalue. The total energy also includes interaction double-counting corrections, so it cannot simply be replaced by the sum of occupied eigenvalues. For a crystal, the next step is to use the periodicity of the self-consistent potential to reduce the infinite system to calculations within a primitive cell.

2. Bloch's theorem: phase changes between cells

Consider a one-dimensional potential with period aaa, and define the translation operator by

V(x+ma)=V(x),T^(a)ψ(x)=ψ(x+a),m∈Z.V(x+ma)=V(x),\qquad \hat T(a)\psi(x)=\psi(x+a),\qquad m\in\mathbb Z. V(x+ma)=V(x),T^(a)ψ(x)=ψ(x+a),m∈Z.

A rigid translation leaves the kinetic energy unchanged, and a lattice translation also leaves the potential unchanged. Thus,

[H^,T^(a)]=0.[\hat H,\hat T(a)]=0. [H^,T^(a)]=0.

The Hamiltonian and translation operator can have simultaneous eigenstates. When degeneracies occur, suitable linear combinations can be chosen within each degenerate subspace. Translation preserves the norm, so its eigenvalues have unit magnitude and can be written as phase factors:

T^(a)ψk=λψk,∣λ∣=1,λ=eika.\hat T(a)\psi_k=\lambda\psi_k, \qquad |\lambda|=1, \qquad \lambda=e^{ika}. T^(a)ψk​=λψk​,∣λ∣=1,λ=eika.

Translation through mmm cells gives

ψk(x+ma)=eikmaψk(x).\psi_k(x+ma)=e^{ikma}\psi_k(x). ψk​(x+ma)=eikmaψk​(x).

kkk is the wave vector, with dimensions of inverse length; ℏk\hbar kℏk is called crystal momentum. In a periodic potential, crystal momentum generally differs from the mechanical momentum of a free particle.

Define unk(x)=e−ikxψnk(x)u_{nk}(x)=e^{-ikx}\psi_{nk}(x)unk​(x)=e−ikxψnk​(x) and substitute the translation relation to obtain the Bloch form:

ψnk(x)=eikxunk(x),unk(x+ma)=unk(x).\psi_{nk}(x)=e^{ikx}u_{nk}(x), \qquad u_{nk}(x+ma)=u_{nk}(x). ψnk​(x)=eikxunk​(x),unk​(x+ma)=unk​(x).

A Bloch state is a plane wave multiplied by a lattice-periodic function. The plane wave records the phase between cells, while the periodic function describes the electronic distribution within a cell. nnn labels the bands, and a single kkk can correspond to several energy eigenstates. Since unku_{nk}unk​ is generally not constant, a Bloch wave is not simply a free-electron plane wave.

For example, when k=π/(2a)k=\pi/(2a)k=π/(2a), translation through one cell gives iψ(x)i\psi(x)iψ(x), two cells give −ψ(x)-\psi(x)−ψ(x), and four cells restore the original phase. Yet each cell translation satisfies

∣ψ(x+a)∣2=∣ψ(x)∣2.|\psi(x+a)|^2=|\psi(x)|^2. ∣ψ(x+a)∣2=∣ψ(x)∣2.

The wavefunction's phase can change while the probability density retains period aaa. Calculating one primitive cell also does not make it an isolated molecule: all translated copies remain connected through the Bloch boundary phase.

3. Reciprocal lattice vectors and the one-dimensional Brillouin zone

If two wave vectors differ by

G=2πma,G=\frac{2\pi m}{a}, G=a2πm​,

then

ei(k+G)a=eika.e^{i(k+G)a}=e^{ika}. ei(k+G)a=eika.

GGG is a reciprocal lattice vector. kkk and k+Gk+Gk+G give the same phase under every lattice translation, so they can label the same physical state. Relabeling also requires changing the periodic part:

un,k+G(x)=e−iGxunk(x),ψn,k+G(x)=ψnk(x).u_{n,k+G}(x)=e^{-iGx}u_{nk}(x), \qquad \psi_{n,k+G}(x)=\psi_{nk}(x). un,k+G​(x)=e−iGxunk​(x),ψn,k+G​(x)=ψnk​(x).

The periodic part cancels the additional plane-wave factor. The energy spectrum therefore has reciprocal-lattice periodicity:

En(k+G)=En(k).E_n(k+G)=E_n(k). En​(k+G)=En​(k).

A nonredundant set of wave vectors can consequently be placed in an interval of width 2π/a2\pi/a2π/a. The usual first Brillouin zone (first BZ) is

−πa≤k<πa.-\frac{\pi}{a}\leq k<\frac{\pi}{a}. −aπ​≤k<aπ​.

The endpoints are equivalent, so a half-open interval avoids double counting. A longer real-space period gives a narrower reciprocal-space interval. When a supercell is used, the bands fold into its smaller BZ; this is called band folding.

For example, if a=0.40 nma=0.40\,\mathrm{nm}a=0.40nm, then G0=15.708 nm−1G_0=15.708\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}G0​=15.708nm−1 and the first BZ is [−7.854,7.854) nm−1[-7.854,7.854)\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}[−7.854,7.854)nm−1. Taking k=12.0 nm−1k=12.0\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}k=12.0nm−1 and subtracting G0G_0G0​ gives the equivalent wave vector k′=−3.708 nm−1k'=-3.708\,\mathrm{nm}^{-1}k′=−3.708nm−1. Folding adds or subtracts reciprocal lattice vectors. Taking the absolute value instead replaces kkk by −k-k−k, which is generally a different state.

4. Three-dimensional lattices, reciprocal space, and primitive cells

An arbitrary translation of a three-dimensional lattice is

R=m1a1+m2a2+m3a3,mi∈Z.\mathbf R=m_1\mathbf a_1+m_2\mathbf a_2+m_3\mathbf a_3, \qquad m_i\in\mathbb Z. R=m1​a1​+m2​a2​+m3​a3​,mi​∈Z.

The primitive real-space vectors ai\mathbf a_iai​ and reciprocal lattice vectors bj\mathbf b_jbj​ satisfy

ai⋅bj=2πδij.\mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf b_j=2\pi\delta_{ij}. ai​⋅bj​=2πδij​.

An arbitrary reciprocal lattice vector is G=∑jhjbj\mathbf G=\sum_j h_j\mathbf b_jG=∑j​hj​bj​, where hjh_jhj​ are integers. Hence,

eiG⋅R=1,e^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf R}=1, eiG⋅R=1,

and the Bloch form becomes

ψnk(r)=eik⋅runk(r),unk(r+R)=unk(r).\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r) =e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r), \qquad u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r). ψnk​(r)=eik⋅runk​(r),unk​(r+R)=unk​(r).

k\mathbf kk and k+G\mathbf k+\mathbf Gk+G remain equivalent labels. The first Brillouin zone is the reciprocal lattice's Wigner–Seitz primitive cell. To construct it, connect the reciprocal-space origin to neighboring lattice points, draw the perpendicular bisector planes of these connections, and take the innermost enclosed region containing the origin. Points inside this region are closer to the origin than to any other reciprocal lattice point.

For a simple cubic lattice with side length aaa, the reciprocal basis vectors have length 2π/a2\pi/a2π/a. The first BZ is a cube whose components satisfy −π/a≤kα<π/a-\pi/a\leq k_\alpha<\pi/a−π/a≤kα​<π/a. Other lattices give different polyhedra: the reciprocal lattice determines the BZ shape.

The Bravais lattice describes translations, while the basis specifies the atoms attached to each lattice point. A primitive cell can contain several atoms without increasing the lattice period. Bloch's theorem restricts the calculation of each unku_{n\mathbf k}unk​ to one primitive cell, but solutions and integration over different k\mathbf kk are still required.

5. Graphene: relating atomic structure to bands

Graphene's honeycomb structure consists of a two-dimensional triangular Bravais lattice with a two-carbon basis. Its primitive cell is the parallelogram spanned by two primitive translation vectors and contains two carbon atoms after accounting for shared boundaries. If the carbon–carbon bond length is ddd, the primitive lattice vectors have length 3 d\sqrt3\,d3​d. The bond length and lattice constant should be distinguished.

The first BZ is a hexagon in reciprocal space. Γ\GammaΓ lies at its center, MMM at an edge midpoint, and KKK and K′K'K′ at alternating corners. The carbon hexagons in real space and the BZ in reciprocal space belong to different spaces.

Bands are commonly plotted along high-symmetry paths such as Γ−M−K−Γ\Gamma-M-K-\GammaΓ−M−K−Γ. The vertical axis is electronic energy, the horizontal axis follows the wave-vector path, and each curve is a band En(k)E_n(\mathbf k)En​(k). Such paths make the bands easy to inspect, but they cannot replace integration over the full BZ when calculating the electron density.

The π\piπ states mainly arise from pzp_zpz​ orbitals perpendicular to the plane, while the σ\sigmaσ bands mainly describe in-plane bonding. An asterisk denotes antibonding character. In ideal graphene, the π\piπ and π∗\pi^*π∗ bands meet near the KKK points, giving a zero band gap. Their approximately linear dispersion near the touching points forms a Dirac cone.

The valence and conduction bands of ideal graphene meet at the K points. This contact occurs at particular wave vectors. Substrates, defects, or structural changes that break the relevant symmetry can alter the bands and require a calculation for the modified structure. The horizontal axis is also not time: electronic energy as a function of wave vector cannot be read as an atomic trajectory.

6. Frozen-core approximation: retaining the core's influence

Core electrons lie close to the nucleus and are tightly bound; valence electrons participate more readily in bonding and charge transfer. The frozen-core approximation holds the shapes of the core orbitals approximately fixed while allowing the valence electrons to change explicitly. The nucleus and frozen core form an effective ionic core, whose charge screening remains part of the potential experienced by the valence electrons.

If the nuclear charge number is ZZZ and the number of frozen core electrons is NcoreN_{\mathrm{core}}Ncore​, then

Zval=Z−Ncore.Z_{\mathrm{val}}=Z-N_{\mathrm{core}}. Zval​=Z−Ncore​.

For example, carbon has nuclear charge +6e+6e+6e. Freezing the two 1s21s^21s2 electrons leaves an effective ionic core with long-range net charge +4e+4e+4e and four explicit valence electrons. Two neutral carbon atoms therefore require eight valence electrons to be treated explicitly. The effective description changes; the nucleus remains a carbon nucleus.

The valence electrons still move in the complete effective potential:

VKS(r)=Vext(r)+VH[ρ](r)+Vxc[ρ](r),V_{\mathrm{KS}}(\mathbf r) =V_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf r) +V_{\mathrm H}[\rho](\mathbf r) +V_{\mathrm{xc}}[\rho](\mathbf r), VKS​(r)=Vext​(r)+VH​[ρ](r)+Vxc​[ρ](r),

VH[ρ](r)=∫ρ(r′)∣r−r′∣ dr′.V_{\mathrm H}[\rho](\mathbf r) =\int\frac{\rho(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}\,d\mathbf r'. VH​[ρ](r)=∫∣r−r′∣ρ(r′)​dr′.

A specific LDA or GGA scheme is chosen for exchange and correlation. If semicore states contribute appreciably to bonding, or high pressure causes core regions to overlap, more electrons should be treated as valence electrons. Freezing the core reduces the number of explicit electrons; pseudopotentials further reduce the cost of representing their valence orbitals.

7. Pseudopotentials: smoothing the core region

Near a nucleus, the true valence wavefunction feels a strong nuclear potential and must remain orthogonal to the core states. It therefore has rapid oscillations and multiple nodes. A plane-wave expansion needs short-wavelength, high-wave-vector components to represent these details, making the calculation expensive.

A pseudopotential replaces the true valence wavefunction in the core region with a smooth pseudo wavefunction. Outside the core cutoff radius rcr_crc​, the required matching is retained:

ψPS(r)≃ψAE(r),r≥rc.\psi^{\mathrm{PS}}(r)\simeq\psi^{\mathrm{AE}}(r), \qquad r\geq r_c. ψPS(r)≃ψAE(r),r≥rc​.

Smoothing the potential and wavefunction inside the core reduces the required high-wave-vector components. An accurate pseudopotential must also preserve bonding information outside the core and scattering properties over the relevant energy range. Here, softening means smoother spatial variation.

Common approaches include:

  • Norm-conserving pseudopotentials preserve the reference state's integrated wavefunction norm inside the core.
  • Ultrasoft pseudopotentials relax this constraint and use augmentation terms to restore the required charge, allowing smoother auxiliary orbitals.
  • PAW (projector augmented-wave) reconstructs all-electron information near each atom from smooth auxiliary states; it is an augmented-wave method.

Transferability means that a pseudopotential generated for a reference atom remains reliable in other bonding environments, oxidation states, and structures. First choose a pseudopotential appropriate for the system, then test whether the numerical cutoff is sufficient. Adding basis functions cannot repair an unsuitable physical approximation.

8. Basis sets, wave-vector sampling, and convergence

The five main inputs to a crystal calculation are the basis set, pseudopotential, exchange-correlation functional, kkk-point sampling, and convergence criteria.

The periodic part of an orbital can be expanded in plane waves:

unk(r)=∑Gcnk(G)eiG⋅r.u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r) =\sum_{\mathbf G}c_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf G)e^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf r}. unk​(r)=G∑​cnk​(G)eiG⋅r.

The components of the full Bloch wave have wave vectors k+G\mathbf k+\mathbf Gk+G and are usually retained according to a kinetic-energy cutoff:

ℏ2∣k+G∣22me≤Ecut.\frac{\hbar^2|\mathbf k+\mathbf G|^2}{2m_e}\leq E_{\mathrm{cut}}. 2me​ℏ2∣k+G∣2​≤Ecut​.

A higher EcutE_{\mathrm{cut}}Ecut​ includes more basis functions and resolves finer spatial variation, at greater computational cost. kkk-point sampling instead approximates BZ integrals using a finite set of wave vectors, for example,

ρ(r)≃∑kwk∑nfnk∣ψnk(r)∣2.\rho(\mathbf r)\simeq \sum_{\mathbf k}w_{\mathbf k}\sum_n f_{n\mathbf k}|\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)|^2. ρ(r)≃k∑​wk​n∑​fnk​∣ψnk​(r)∣2.

wkw_{\mathbf k}wk​ is the integration weight and fnkf_{n\mathbf k}fnk​ the occupation number; their normalization must match the orbital and cell conventions. The cutoff controls the orbital representation at each wave vector, while the kkk mesh controls reciprocal-space integration. They require separate convergence tests.

The pseudopotential specifies the ionic core and explicit valence electrons, while the exchange-correlation functional specifies the many-electron approximation. They should be compatible. Comparisons of structural energies also require comparable electron numbers, energy references, and computational settings.

SCF convergence criteria specify how small the energy or density changes must become before iteration stops. SCF convergence gives a self-consistent solution within the current basis and kkk mesh. The target energy differences, forces, or bands should also remain stable when the cutoff is increased and the mesh refined.

For example, suppose the same energy difference at cutoffs of 300,400,500 eV300,400,500\,\mathrm{eV}300,400,500eV is 0.120,0.103,0.102 eV0.120,0.103,0.102\,\mathrm{eV}0.120,0.103,0.102eV, respectively. If the target error is 0.005 eV0.005\,\mathrm{eV}0.005eV, the last two results differ by only 0.001 eV0.001\,\mathrm{eV}0.001eV, suggesting that this energy difference is reasonably stable with respect to the cutoff. Next, hold the cutoff fixed and test the kkk mesh. Systematic errors from different functionals require a separate assessment.

9. Self-tests

  1. Does ψ(x+a)=−ψ(x)\psi(x+a)=-\psi(x)ψ(x+a)=−ψ(x) violate crystal periodicity? No. It corresponds to eika=−1e^{ika}=-1eika=−1, for example k=π/ak=\pi/ak=π/a; the probability density still has period aaa.
  2. What happens when the same structure is represented by a supercell of period 2a2a2a? The first BZ width decreases from 2π/a2\pi/a2π/a to π/a\pi/aπ/a, and the bands fold. Whether a real new gap appears depends on whether the physical structure changes.
  3. What costs do the frozen-core approximation and pseudopotentials reduce? The former reduces the number of explicitly solved electrons; the latter reduces the basis functions needed to represent the valence wavefunctions.
  4. Why can two SCF-converged calculations give different results? Self-consistency only makes the density and potential agree within each calculation's settings. The basis, wave-vector sampling, pseudopotential, functional, and structure may differ.

IV. Structural Phase Changes and the Adiabatic Approximation

1. Born–Oppenheimer approximation: electrons follow nuclear motion

A band structure is calculated for a specified atomic configuration. Stretching a bond or moving an adsorbed atom changes the electronic potential, so the electronic states and energy must be recalculated. Repeating this for a continuous range of configurations gives the potential energy surface (PES) that governs atomic motion.

Nuclei are much heavier than electrons. In many structural problems, nuclear motion is slow enough for the electrons to adjust to the state associated with the current nuclear configuration. This is the starting point of the Born–Oppenheimer (BO) approximation.

The full Hamiltonian is

H^=T^e+T^N+V^ee+V^Ne+V^NN.\hat H=\hat T_e+\hat T_N+\hat V_{ee}+\hat V_{Ne}+\hat V_{NN}. H^=T^e​+T^N​+V^ee​+V^Ne​+V^NN​.

T^e\hat T_eT^e​ and T^N\hat T_NT^N​ are the electronic and nuclear kinetic energies, respectively; V^ee\hat V_{ee}V^ee​ is electron–electron repulsion, V^Ne\hat V_{Ne}V^Ne​ is nuclear–electron attraction, and V^NN\hat V_{NN}V^NN​ is nuclear repulsion. Let r\mathbf rr denote all electronic coordinates and R\mathbf RR all nuclear coordinates, and use the product form

Ψ(r,R)≃χ(R)ϕe(r;R).\Psi(\mathbf r,\mathbf R)\simeq \chi(\mathbf R)\phi_e(\mathbf r;\mathbf R). Ψ(r,R)≃χ(R)ϕe​(r;R).

First hold R\mathbf RR fixed and solve the electronic equation:

H^e(R)ϕe=Ee(R)ϕe,H^e=T^e+V^ee+V^Ne.\hat H_e(\mathbf R)\phi_e =E_e(\mathbf R)\phi_e, \qquad \hat H_e=\hat T_e+\hat V_{ee}+\hat V_{Ne}. H^e​(R)ϕe​=Ee​(R)ϕe​,H^e​=T^e​+V^ee​+V^Ne​.

The semicolon indicates that the nuclear coordinates are parameters in the electronic equation. Here, DFT/KS is usually used to obtain the electronic ground state. At fixed nuclear coordinates, VNNV_{NN}VNN​ is a constant and does not change the electronic state, so it can be separated from the electronic equation.

When the product wavefunction is substituted into the full equation, the nuclear kinetic-energy operator differentiates with respect to R\mathbf RR and acts on both χ\chiχ and ϕe\phi_eϕe​. The BO approximation neglects the associated electronic-state derivatives and nonadiabatic coupling, approximately confining nuclear motion to a single electronic potential energy surface:

[T^N+VNN(R)+Ee(R)]χ(R)=Eχ(R).\left[\hat T_N+V_{NN}(\mathbf R)+E_e(\mathbf R)\right] \chi(\mathbf R)=E\chi(\mathbf R). [T^N​+VNN​(R)+Ee​(R)]χ(R)=Eχ(R).

The electrons are assumed to adjust adiabatically to the nuclear configuration. Here, adiabatic means that the electrons approximately remain in the selected electronic state as the nuclei move slowly. It differs from a thermodynamically adiabatic process, which exchanges no heat with its surroundings.

This is still a quantum equation for the nuclei. A further classical-nuclei approximation replaces the nuclear wavefunction with positions and velocities. BO separation and classical nuclear dynamics are distinct approximations: zero-point motion and tunneling require a quantum treatment of the nuclei, while near-degenerate electronic states or significant electronic transitions require coupling between multiple electronic states.

2. From electronic energy to atomic forces

The potential energy experienced by the nuclei is the electronic energy plus nuclear repulsion:

U(R)=Ee(R)+VNN(R).U(\mathbf R)=E_e(\mathbf R)+V_{NN}(\mathbf R). U(R)=Ee​(R)+VNN​(R).

For NNN atoms, R\mathbf RR contains all 3N3N3N coordinate components. The atomic force is the negative gradient with respect to an atom's position:

Fi=−∇RiU=FiNN−∇RiEe,FiNN=−∇RiVNN.\mathbf F_i=-\nabla_{\mathbf R_i}U =\mathbf F_i^{NN}-\nabla_{\mathbf R_i}E_e, \qquad \mathbf F_i^{NN}=-\nabla_{\mathbf R_i}V_{NN}. Fi​=−∇Ri​​U=FiNN​−∇Ri​​Ee​,FiNN​=−∇Ri​​VNN​.

If the electronic-structure program's total energy already includes nuclear repulsion, it should not be added again. The minus sign makes the force point locally toward lower potential energy. When energy is measured in eV\mathrm{eV}eV and position in A˚\text{Å}A˚, the force unit is eV/A˚\mathrm{eV}/\text{Å}eV/A˚.

With classical nuclei, Newton's equation advances the trajectory:

MiR¨i(t)=Fi.M_i\ddot{\mathbf R}_i(t)=\mathbf F_i. Mi​R¨i​(t)=Fi​.

The Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics cycle is: fix the current configuration, solve self-consistently for the electronic ground state, calculate forces, move the atoms, and solve the electronic problem again for the new configuration. The electronic state changes along the trajectory, but a stationary electronic equation is solved at each step.

Consider a one-dimensional bond extension:

U(x)=12κ(x−x0)2,F(x)=−κ(x−x0).U(x)=\frac12\kappa(x-x_0)^2, \qquad F(x)=-\kappa(x-x_0). U(x)=21​κ(x−x0​)2,F(x)=−κ(x−x0​).

Take κ=4 eV/A˚2\kappa=4\,\mathrm{eV}/\text{Å}^2κ=4eV/A˚2 and x0=1.50 A˚x_0=1.50\,\text{Å}x0​=1.50A˚. At x=1.60 A˚x=1.60\,\text{Å}x=1.60A˚, the force is F=−0.40 eV/A˚F=-0.40\,\mathrm{eV}/\text{Å}F=−0.40eV/A˚, accelerating the atom toward smaller xxx. At x0x_0x0​ the force is zero and the curvature is positive, so this is a stable minimum. Maxima and saddle points on a general potential energy surface can also have zero force; stability additionally depends on curvature.

Electronic self-consistency, mechanical equilibrium, and finite-temperature equilibrium are different conditions. Electronic self-consistency requires a compatible density and potential; mechanical equilibrium requires zero net atomic forces; thermal equilibrium allows continued atomic motion. Even when starting from a zero-temperature static-structure problem, atoms displaced from equilibrium experience forces and accelerate.

Force determines acceleration, while velocity also depends on the preceding motion. An atom can therefore pass through a minimum by inertia even when the force points toward lower potential energy. Undamped dynamics exchanges kinetic and potential energy. Structural optimization instead requires an energy-minimization algorithm or dissipation to bring the system to rest near a stable structure.

3. Hellmann–Feynman theorem and Pulay forces

When differentiating energy with respect to position, both the Hamiltonian and the electronic wavefunction change. Let λ\lambdaλ be one nuclear coordinate component, and normalize the electronic state:

Ee(λ)=⟨ϕ(λ)∣H^e(λ)∣ϕ(λ)⟩,⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=1.E_e(\lambda)= \langle\phi(\lambda)|\hat H_e(\lambda)|\phi(\lambda)\rangle, \qquad \langle\phi|\phi\rangle=1. Ee​(λ)=⟨ϕ(λ)∣H^e​(λ)∣ϕ(λ)⟩,⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩=1.

Differentiate the bra, Hamiltonian, and ket separately. Since the Hamiltonian is Hermitian, the two wavefunction-derivative terms combine into twice their real part:

dEedλ=⟨ϕ∣∂H^e∂λ∣ϕ⟩+2Re⁡⟨∂ϕ∂λ|H^e|ϕ⟩.\frac{dE_e}{d\lambda} =\left\langle\phi\left| \frac{\partial\hat H_e}{\partial\lambda} \right|\phi\right\rangle +2\operatorname{Re} \left\langle\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\lambda} \middle|\hat H_e\middle|\phi\right\rangle. dλdEe​​=⟨ϕ∣∣∣∣∣∣​∂λ∂H^e​​∣∣∣∣∣∣​ϕ⟩+2Re⟨∂λ∂ϕ​∣∣∣∣∣​H^e​∣∣∣∣∣​ϕ⟩.

If H^e∣ϕ⟩=Ee∣ϕ⟩\hat H_e|\phi\rangle=E_e|\phi\rangleH^e​∣ϕ⟩=Ee​∣ϕ⟩, the wavefunction-derivative terms sum to

Eed⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩dλ=0.E_e\frac{d\langle\phi|\phi\rangle}{d\lambda}=0. Ee​dλd⟨ϕ∣ϕ⟩​=0.

The cancellation follows from the eigenvalue equation and normalization; the wavefunction itself still changes with nuclear position. This gives the Hellmann–Feynman theorem:

dEedλ=⟨ϕ∣∂H^e∂λ∣ϕ⟩,\frac{dE_e}{d\lambda} =\left\langle\phi\left| \frac{\partial\hat H_e}{\partial\lambda} \right|\phi\right\rangle, dλdEe​​=⟨ϕ∣∣∣∣∣∣​∂λ∂H^e​​∣∣∣∣∣∣​ϕ⟩,

Fi=FiNN−⟨ϕe∣∇RiH^e∣ϕe⟩.\mathbf F_i= \mathbf F_i^{NN} -\left\langle\phi_e\left| \nabla_{\mathbf R_i}\hat H_e \right|\phi_e\right\rangle. Fi​=FiNN​−⟨ϕe​∣∣∣∣​∇Ri​​H^e​∣∣∣∣​ϕe​⟩.

In DFT, the corresponding argument uses the variational stationarity of the self-consistent electronic solution. The quantity being differentiated must be the complete total-energy functional.

A finite basis can also produce a Pulay force. For example, atom-centered orbitals move with their atoms, so the finite variational space changes with the structure. Differentiating only the Hamiltonian's explicit coordinate dependence omits this contribution. It vanishes in the complete-basis limit.

A pure plane-wave basis in a fixed cell does not change with atomic displacement and usually has no such atomic-displacement Pulay term. Changing the cell can instead introduce Pulay stress. Force errors caused by incomplete electronic self-consistency have a different origin from basis-dependent Pulay terms and should be treated separately.

Accurate forces must be consistent with the calculated total energy. Before using forces to optimize a structure or advance dynamics, converge the electronic calculation and include the corrections required by the basis.

4. Velocity Verlet time integration

For position-dependent conservative forces, Velocity Verlet divides the velocity update into two half steps. Let nnn label the time step and Δt\Delta tΔt be its size. The update sequence is

vin+1/2=vin+Δt2MiFin,\mathbf v_i^{n+1/2} =\mathbf v_i^n+\frac{\Delta t}{2M_i}\mathbf F_i^n, vin+1/2​=vin​+2Mi​Δt​Fin​,

Rin+1=Rin+Δt vin+1/2,\mathbf R_i^{n+1} =\mathbf R_i^n+\Delta t\,\mathbf v_i^{n+1/2}, Rin+1​=Rin​+Δtvin+1/2​,

Fin+1=−∇RiU(Rn+1),\mathbf F_i^{n+1} =-\nabla_{\mathbf R_i}U(\mathbf R^{n+1}), Fin+1​=−∇Ri​​U(Rn+1),

vin+1=vin+1/2+Δt2MiFin+1.\mathbf v_i^{n+1} =\mathbf v_i^{n+1/2}+\frac{\Delta t}{2M_i}\mathbf F_i^{n+1}. vin+1​=vin+1/2​+2Mi​Δt​Fin+1​.

This is half kick, drift, recalculate forces, half kick: use the old force to update the velocity by half a step, move the atoms, recalculate the force, and complete the remaining half step. The new force depends on all the new coordinates. In BO MD, this requires electronic self-consistency for the new configuration first.

Substituting the first equation into the second gives the familiar position update:

Rin+1=Rin+vinΔt+Fin2MiΔt2.\mathbf R_i^{n+1} =\mathbf R_i^n+\mathbf v_i^n\Delta t +\frac{\mathbf F_i^n}{2M_i}\Delta t^2. Rin+1​=Rin​+vin​Δt+2Mi​Fin​​Δt2.

The final velocity update must use the new force at t+Δtt+\Delta tt+Δt. Velocity Verlet uses forces at both ends of the time step and is a second-order integration method.

One complete step for a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator

Use reduced units with M=1M=1M=1 and U(x)=x2/2U(x)=x^2/2U(x)=x2/2, so F=−xF=-xF=−x. Start from x0=1x^0=1x0=1 and v0=0v^0=0v0=0, with Δt=0.10\Delta t=0.10Δt=0.10:

F0=−1,v1/2=−0.05,x1=0.995,F^0=-1,\qquad v^{1/2}=-0.05,\qquad x^1=0.995, F0=−1,v1/2=−0.05,x1=0.995,

F1=−0.995,v1=−0.09975.F^1=-0.995,\qquad v^1=-0.09975. F1=−0.995,v1=−0.09975.

The initial total energy is 0.50.50.5. After one step, the potential energy is approximately 0.49501250.49501250.4950125, the kinetic energy 0.00497500.00497500.0049750, and the total energy 0.49998750.49998750.4999875. Most of the decrease in potential energy becomes kinetic energy; the atom does not automatically stop at the minimum.

The time step must resolve the fastest relevant motion. An excessively large Δt\Delta tΔt increases error and can destabilize the integration, while an excessively small step increases computational cost. For a conservative system, check the long-term numerical stability of K+UK+UK+U. Velocity-dependent thermostat forces require integration steps appropriate to the thermostat.

5. Nosé–Hoover thermostat and finite temperature

The NVT, or canonical, ensemble fixes particle number, volume, and bath temperature. The system itself can exchange energy with the bath. At equilibrium, atoms continue to move, and instantaneous temperature and energy fluctuate.

Kinetic energy, temperature, and degrees of freedom

Define the nuclear kinetic energy and instantaneous temperature by

K=∑i12Mi∣vi∣2,Tinst=2KgkB.K=\sum_i\frac12M_i|\mathbf v_i|^2, \qquad T_{\mathrm{inst}}=\frac{2K}{gk_{\mathrm B}}. K=i∑​21​Mi​∣vi​∣2,Tinst​=gkB​2K​.

ggg is the number of independent momentum degrees of freedom associated with thermal motion. For an unconstrained three-dimensional system, start from 3N3N3N and subtract the degrees removed by center-of-mass translation removal or other constraints. At the target temperature T0T_0T0​, the mean kinetic energy satisfies

⟨K⟩=g2kBT0.\langle K\rangle=\frac g2k_{\mathrm B}T_0. ⟨K⟩=2g​kB​T0​.

Initial velocities can be sampled from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. For a velocity component α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,zα=x,y,z,

p(viα)=Mi2πkBT0exp⁡(−Miviα22kBT0).p(v_{i\alpha}) =\sqrt{\frac{M_i}{2\pi k_{\mathrm B}T_0}} \exp\left(-\frac{M_iv_{i\alpha}^2}{2k_{\mathrm B}T_0}\right). p(viα​)=2πkB​T0​Mi​​​exp(−2kB​T0​Mi​viα2​​).

Each component has zero mean and variance kBT0/Mik_{\mathrm B}T_0/M_ikB​T0​/Mi​, so heavier atoms have smaller typical speeds at the same temperature. After velocity initialization, the structure and its modes of motion still require an equilibration period.

For example, removing overall translation from ten atoms in three dimensions gives g=27g=27g=27. If K=0.349 eVK=0.349\,\mathrm{eV}K=0.349eV, using kB=8.6173×10−5 eV/Kk_{\mathrm B}=8.6173\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{eV/K}kB​=8.6173×10−5eV/K gives Tinst≈300 KT_{\mathrm{inst}}\approx300\,\mathrm KTinst​≈300K. Incorrectly using g=30g=30g=30 would instead give approximately 270 K270\,\mathrm K270K.

How dynamic friction heats and cools

A common single-bath form of the Nosé–Hoover equations is

MiR¨i=Fi−ξMivi,ξ˙=2K−gkBT0Q.M_i\ddot{\mathbf R}_i =\mathbf F_i-\xi M_i\mathbf v_i, \qquad \dot\xi=\frac{2K-gk_{\mathrm B}T_0}{Q}. Mi​R¨i​=Fi​−ξMi​vi​,ξ˙​=Q2K−gkB​T0​​.

ξ\xiξ is the dynamic friction coefficient. Q>0Q>0Q>0 is the thermostat mass, which controls the adjustment timescale and has dimensions of energy times time squared. For ξ>0\xi>0ξ>0, the added force opposes velocity and removes kinetic energy; for ξ<0\xi<0ξ<0, it adds kinetic energy:

dKdt∣thermostat=−2ξK.\left.\frac{dK}{dt}\right|_{\mathrm{thermostat}} =-2\xi K. dtdK​∣∣∣∣∣​thermostat​=−2ξK.

Excess kinetic energy makes ξ˙>0\dot\xi>0ξ˙​>0, driving the friction coefficient upward; insufficient kinetic energy drives it downward. ξ˙\dot\xiξ˙​ determines how the coefficient changes, whereas the sign of ξ\xiξ determines whether the thermostat is currently heating or cooling.

The equilibrium objective is a mean kinetic energy corresponding to T0T_0T0​ and the appropriate statistical distribution. Correct sampling also requires stable integration and sufficient exploration of accessible states. In simple systems, a single Nosé–Hoover thermostat may need to be extended to a thermostat chain to improve sampling.

An extended-system form using βi\beta_iβi​ is

β˙i(t)=1τ[K−3N+12kBT0].\dot\beta_i(t) =\frac1\tau\left[K-\frac{3N+1}{2}k_{\mathrm B}T_0\right]. β˙​i​(t)=τ1​[K−23N+1​kB​T0​].

This uses different parameter and degree-of-freedom conventions from the standard ξ,g,Q\xi,g,Qξ,g,Q form. Dimensional analysis of this equation gives τ\tauτ units of energy times time squared. The instantaneous atomic temperature still uses the actual thermal degrees of freedom ggg. When applying a particular thermostat equation, use its own parameter definitions.

6. Pt-induced Ge nanowires: atomic rearrangement during motion

Pt-induced nanowires on Ge(001) connect electronic structure, atomic forces, and structural transformations. Neighboring wires are separated by approximately 16 A˚16\,\text{Å}16A˚. Pt-induced means that adding Pt induces the nanowires to form. The wires include Ge atoms rearranged from the substrate, and surrounding Pt–Ge bonds help stabilize this arrangement. Vanpoucke & Brocks, 2008

This surface also provides a setting for CO oxidation:

2CO+O2→2CO2.2\mathrm{CO}+\mathrm O_2\rightarrow2\mathrm{CO}_2. 2CO+O2​→2CO2​.

The coordination environment determines which surface atoms bond to an adsorbed molecule, so reconstruction can also change catalytic activity. Xi, Guo & Zhang, 2016

Relating energy changes to structural changes

The horizontal axis of the energy trajectory is actual MD simulation time, measured in fs\mathrm{fs}fs. Since 1000 fs=1 ps1000\,\mathrm{fs}=1\,\mathrm{ps}1000fs=1ps, the full trajectory covers about 3 ps3\,\mathrm{ps}3ps. The initial PINW structure vibrates around a higher energy level, enters the transition region between approximately 500500500 and 1300 fs1300\,\mathrm{fs}1300fs, and then fluctuates around the lower level associated with PGNW.

Representative energies before and after the transition are approximately −346.6-346.6−346.6 and −347.5 eV-347.5\,\mathrm{eV}−347.5eV, differing by about 0.9 eV0.9\,\mathrm{eV}0.9eV.
