This is the difference between the energy levels of the two stages. A reaction barrier is instead the energy rise from the initial state to the transition state along a path.

Snapshots at 000, 500500500, 128912891289, and 3000 fs3000\,\mathrm{fs}3000fs show positions and connections changing within the same local region, with a new wire arrangement retained at later times. Vibrations continue within each stage; the structural transformation is the change from one atomic arrangement to another.

In BO MD, each step first obtains the electronic ground-state energy of the current configuration, calculates forces from its gradient, and then advances the atoms. As atoms approach or separate, orbital overlap and coordination change, and new bonding takes the system into another low-energy region. The energy curve tells us when a change occurs; coordinates, bond lengths, and coordination tell us what changes.

Adsorption and surface reconstruction affect each other

As O2\mathrm O_2O2​ approaches the Ge wire, Ge atoms can rearrange to form a new adsorption configuration. Xi, Guo & Zhang, 2016, Supporting Information

The molecule and surface jointly determine the potential energy surface. When adsorption creates new bonds, the original local equilibrium positions also change. Relaxing the relevant surface atoms together with the molecule gives the jointly stable structure of the adsorbate and reconstructed surface.

7. Self-tests

  1. Does the BO approximation necessarily make the nuclei classical? No. BO first provides an electronic potential energy surface, on which the nuclei can still be treated quantum mechanically. Newtonian trajectories follow only after the additional classical-nuclei approximation.
  2. Why does the Hellmann–Feynman formula hold when the electronic wavefunction changes with atomic position? For an exact normalized eigenstate, the wavefunction-derivative terms cancel through the eigenvalue equation and normalization. A finite, position-dependent basis requires Pulay corrections.
  3. Which force is used in the final Velocity Verlet half step? The force at the new positions, Fin+1\mathbf F_i^{n+1}Fin+1​, obtained after updating positions and recalculating the forces.
  4. Are temperature fluctuations and a nonconstant system energy normal in NVT simulations? They can be. The system exchanges energy with the bath, and the equilibrium ensemble allows fluctuations. Check the averages, distributions, sampling, and integration stability.

V. Thermal Catalysis

1. From electronic energy to chemical reactions

At fixed atomic positions, first solve for the electronic ground state. After the atoms move, solve for the new ground state. Under the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, the electronic ground-state energy Ee(R)E_e(\mathbf R)Ee​(R) and the nuclear repulsion energy together define the potential energy surface on which the nuclei move:

EBO(R)=Ee(R)+VNN(R).E_{\mathrm{BO}}(\mathbf R)=E_e(\mathbf R)+V_{\mathrm{NN}}(\mathbf R). EBO​(R)=Ee​(R)+VNN​(R).

The force on an atom is the negative gradient of the total potential energy with respect to its nuclear coordinates:

FI=−∇IEBO=FINN−∇IEe,MIR¨I=FI.\mathbf F_I=-\nabla_I E_{\mathrm{BO}} =\mathbf F_I^{\mathrm{NN}}-\nabla_I E_e, \qquad M_I\ddot{\mathbf R}_I=\mathbf F_I. FI​=−∇I​EBO​=FINN​−∇I​Ee​,MI​R¨I​=FI​.

III labels an atom, MIM_IMI​ is its mass, and FINN\mathbf F_I^{\mathrm{NN}}FINN​ is the force due to nuclear repulsion. The minus sign makes the force point toward locally decreasing energy. Electronic self-consistency solves the electronic problem at the current nuclear coordinates; structural convergence additionally requires sufficiently small forces on the atoms that are allowed to move.

The same energies and forces serve different purposes. Structure optimization finds stable geometries; molecular dynamics advances positions and velocities in time using the atomic masses; reaction-path calculations search for a route across the barrier between two stable structures. Ordinary minimization stops in the reactant energy minimum, and short MD trajectories often miss rare barrier-crossing events. Dedicated path-search methods are therefore needed.

Thermal catalysis asks three questions: which bond must be activated, how the catalyst helps it rearrange, and how high a barrier the reaction must cross. Atomic positions reveal changes in bonding, while the energy profile gives their energetic cost. Together, they describe the reaction mechanism.

2. Why exothermic reactions still have barriers

The local minimum containing the reactants is the initial state (IS), and the product minimum is the final state (FS). The connecting path usually passes through a transition state (TS). The energy difference from the current reactant minimum to the TS is the activation barrier:

Ea=ETS−EIS.E_a=E_{\mathrm{TS}}-E_{\mathrm{IS}}. Ea​=ETS​−EIS​.

Low product energy establishes only that the overall reaction releases energy. Before new bonds can form, the system often has to weaken existing bonds and rearrange its geometry, producing an energy maximum along the way. A reaction coordinate orders these configurations by reaction progress. It may be a bond length or distance along the path; it is not elapsed time.

The high-energy tail of the thermal distribution allows a small fraction of the ensemble to cross the barrier. Raising the temperature increases this fraction. A catalyst instead provides an alternative path with a lower barrier through adsorption, electron transfer, and intermediate formation. The available sites are regenerated after a complete catalytic cycle. For the same net reaction and thermodynamic initial and final states, the catalyst speeds up equilibration while leaving the reaction free energy and equilibrium constant unchanged.

The three types of catalysis differ in how the reaction is driven: thermocatalysis relies on thermal activation, electrocatalysis uses an applied potential to control electron transfer, and photocatalysis uses photoexcitation. This chapter focuses on thermally activated reactions.

3. Fe2C12\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm C_{12}Fe2​C12​: Donating electrons to oxygen antibonding orbitals

The activity of two-dimensional Fe2C12\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm C_{12}Fe2​C12​ comes from its exposed Fe sites. They donate electrons to the oxygen molecule's 2π∗2\pi^*2π∗ antibonding orbitals, weakening the O–O bond and making oxygen more reactive toward CO. Each primitive cell contains two Fe atoms and twelve C atoms. Each Fe is coordinated to three C atoms, with Fe atoms protruding on opposite sides of the carbon plane. The carbon network anchors Fe and adjusts its electronic states through coordination, creating single-atom active sites. Li et al. (2021)

Fe sites donate electrons to oxygen antibonding states. In the charge-density difference isosurfaces, yellow indicates electron accumulation and cyan indicates depletion.

Why oxygen becomes activated

The Fe magnetic moment is approximately 1μB1\mu_{\mathrm B}1μB​ per atom and 2μB2\mu_{\mathrm B}2μB​ per primitive cell. Near the Fermi energy EFE_{\mathrm F}EF​, the spin-down E1E_1E1​ states are partially occupied and can donate electrons to empty oxygen antibonding states. After side-on adsorption, oxygen gains approximately 0.78∣e∣0.78|e|0.78∣e∣. The O–O bond length increases from 1.231.231.23 to 1.40 A˚1.40\,\text{\AA}1.40A˚, while the oxygen magnetic moment decreases from 2.02.02.0 to 0.55μB0.55\mu_{\mathrm B}0.55μB​.

This electron transfer can be understood through the charge-density difference and the projected density of states (PDOS). The charge-density difference is defined as:

Δρ(r)=ρcombined(r)−ρcatalyst(r)−ρadsorbate(r).\Delta\rho(\mathbf r) =\rho_{\mathrm{combined}}(\mathbf r) -\rho_{\mathrm{catalyst}}(\mathbf r) -\rho_{\mathrm{adsorbate}}(\mathbf r). Δρ(r)=ρcombined​(r)−ρcatalyst​(r)−ρadsorbate​(r).

The separated fragments and the combined system use the same atomic positions and computational settings. Δρ>0\Delta\rho>0Δρ>0 indicates local electron accumulation after adsorption, and Δρ<0\Delta\rho<0Δρ<0 indicates depletion.

The PDOS displays oxygen-related electronic states as a function of E−EFE-E_{\mathrm F}E−EF​. Before adsorption, the spin-down 2π∗2\pi^*2π∗ states are empty. After adsorption, some of these states move below the Fermi energy and become occupied. The additional antibonding electrons weaken the net bonding, lengthening O–O. Spin-resolved PDOS plots often place the two channels on opposite sides of zero; the downward-mirrored curve still represents a positive density of states.

One oxygen molecule oxidizes two CO molecules in sequence

The first stage releases one carbon dioxide molecule and leaves adsorbed oxygen; the second removes the remaining oxygen. Each local barrier is measured from its preceding energy minimum.

CO and oxygen first coadsorb on Fe and then react through a Langmuir–Hinshelwood (LH) mechanism. They rearrange to form an OCOO intermediate, pass through the first transition state, and enter a metastable intermediate minimum (MS). O–O then stretches further and breaks through the second transition state, releasing the first carbon dioxide molecule:

COads+O2,ads⟶CO2+Oads.\mathrm{CO}_{\mathrm{ads}}+\mathrm O_{2,\mathrm{ads}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2+\mathrm O_{\mathrm{ads}}. COads​+O2,ads​⟶CO2​+Oads​.

The vacuum path used for comparison in this example has a barrier of approximately 3 eV3\,\mathrm{eV}3eV. The catalytic path divides the reaction into more accessible steps, with the two local barriers equal to 0.440.440.44 and 0.38 eV0.38\,\mathrm{eV}0.38eV. A second CO then reacts with the remaining adsorbed oxygen, crossing a barrier of 0.48 eV0.48\,\mathrm{eV}0.48eV:

CO+Oads⟶CO2.\mathrm{CO}+\mathrm O_{\mathrm{ads}}\longrightarrow\mathrm{CO}_2. CO+Oads​⟶CO2​.

Adding the two stages gives the net reaction:

2CO+O2⟶2CO2.2\mathrm{CO}+\mathrm O_2\longrightarrow2\mathrm{CO}_2. 2CO+O2​⟶2CO2​.

The adsorption energy of CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ on Fe is only approximately −0.03 eV-0.03\,\mathrm{eV}−0.03eV, so the product binds weakly and can leave readily. The catalyst thus meets three requirements: it activates oxygen, provides low barriers for subsequent reactions, and allows product desorption to restore the site.

Each barrier is measured from its preceding energy minimum:

Ea,1=ETS1−EIS,Ea,2=ETS2−EMS.E_{a,1}=E_{\mathrm{TS}_1}-E_{\mathrm{IS}}, \qquad E_{a,2}=E_{\mathrm{TS}_2}-E_{\mathrm{MS}}. Ea,1​=ETS1​​−EIS​,Ea,2​=ETS2​​−EMS​.

For example, if MS lies at −0.60 eV-0.60\,\mathrm{eV}−0.60eV and the following TS lies at −0.22 eV-0.22\,\mathrm{eV}−0.22eV, the local barrier is still 0.38 eV0.38\,\mathrm{eV}0.38eV. A later maximum below the original IS does not make the step from the current intermediate barrierless. When the two stages are plotted separately, each can use its own initial state as zero. Combining them into one energy profile requires a consistent reference for the adsorbates, gas-phase molecules, and catalyst.

For the Eley–Rideal (ER) mechanism, in which gas-phase CO directly attacks adsorbed oxygen, the first-stage barrier is 0.79 eV0.79\,\mathrm{eV}0.79eV. The coadsorbed LH first stage is therefore easier to cross. The rate of the complete cycle also depends on the populations of the adsorbed states and the kinetic prefactors. Li et al. (2021)

4. The Arrhenius relation: how barriers affect rates

A thermally activated rate can be understood as the attempt rate multiplied by the fraction of successful barrier crossings. For an energy barrier EaE_aEa​ per reaction event, the Arrhenius equation is:

k=Aexp⁡ ⁣(−EakBT).k=A\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_a}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right). k=Aexp(−kB​TEa​​).

kkk is the rate constant, and AAA is the pre-exponential factor, which includes the attempt frequency, orientation, and statistical factors. AAA and kkk have the same units, usually s−1\mathrm{s}^{-1}s−1 for a first-order reaction or a simple hopping process. The full reaction rate also includes reactant concentrations or surface coverages.

The exponent must be dimensionless. When EaE_aEa​ is given per reaction event in eV, kBk_{\mathrm B}kB​ must be in eV/K and TTT in K. For a molar activation energy, use the gas constant RRR instead:

k=Aexp⁡ ⁣(−Ea,molRT).k=A\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{a,\mathrm{mol}}}{RT}\right). k=Aexp(−RTEa,mol​​).

For example, convert 50 kJ mol−150\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}50kJmol−1 to 50000 J mol−150000\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}50000Jmol−1 before combining it with RTRTRT expressed in joule-based units.

Taking the logarithm gives:

ln⁡k=ln⁡A−EakB1T.\ln k=\ln A-\frac{E_a}{k_{\mathrm B}}\frac{1}{T}. lnk=lnA−kB​Ea​​T1​.

Over a temperature range in which the mechanism, AAA, and EaE_aEa​ remain approximately constant, plotting ln⁡k\ln klnk against 1/T1/T1/T gives a straight line with slope −Ea/kB-E_a/k_{\mathrm B}−Ea​/kB​. A slope of −6000 K-6000\,\mathrm K−6000K therefore gives Ea≈0.517 eVE_a\approx0.517\,\mathrm{eV}Ea​≈0.517eV.

To compare two paths at the same temperature:

k2k1=A2A1exp⁡ ⁣(Ea,1−Ea,2kBT).\frac{k_2}{k_1} =\frac{A_2}{A_1} \exp\!\left(\frac{E_{a,1}-E_{a,2}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right). k1​k2​​=A1​A2​​exp(kB​TEa,1​−Ea,2​​).

Equal prefactors cancel. At 300 K300\,\mathrm K300K, kBT≈0.02585 eVk_{\mathrm B}T\approx0.02585\,\mathrm{eV}kB​T≈0.02585eV. Lowering the barrier from 0.500.500.50 to 0.40 eV0.40\,\mathrm{eV}0.40eV increases the rate constant by:

knewkold=exp⁡ ⁣(0.100.02585)≈47.9.\frac{k_{\mathrm{new}}}{k_{\mathrm{old}}} =\exp\!\left(\frac{0.10}{0.02585}\right) \approx47.9. kold​knew​​=exp(0.025850.10​)≈47.9.

For the same process at two temperatures, taking AAA and EaE_aEa​ as constant gives:

ln⁡k(T2)k(T1)=EakB(1T1−1T2).\ln\frac{k(T_2)}{k(T_1)} =\frac{E_a}{k_{\mathrm B}} \left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right). lnk(T1​)k(T2​)​=kB​Ea​​(T1​1​−T2​1​).

Increasing the temperature makes the right-hand side positive, so the rate increases. DFT paths usually provide electronic energy differences. Quantitative finite-temperature rates may additionally require vibrational, entropic, and free-energy contributions.

5. Why metals are useful, and why adsorption must not be too strong

Metals have states near the Fermi energy that can donate or accept electrons. Upon contact with a reactant, these states hybridize with molecular orbitals, allowing existing bonds to weaken and new bonds to form. Electron transfer depends on energy alignment, occupation, and orbital overlap: a metal can donate to unoccupied or partially occupied molecular orbitals, while the molecule can also donate back to the metal.

For a finite cluster, the HOMO–LUMO gap is the energy difference between the highest occupied molecular orbital and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital. Small Fe, Au, and Pt clusters have relatively small gaps and can often rearrange electrons at low energetic cost. Changing the atom count changes coordination and orbital splitting, so the gap can vary nonmonotonically with cluster size.

A small gap indicates that electrons can redistribute relatively easily. Catalysis also requires effective coupling to the target reactant and suitable binding strengths. Ligands that constrain Co coordination, or a carbon network that embeds metal atoms, can adjust orbital splitting, reactant approach directions, and binding through the surrounding atoms and bond angles.

The Sabatier principle requires binding that is neither too weak nor too strong. Weak reactant adsorption gives low coverage and makes effective electron transfer difficult. Strongly bound intermediates or products can occupy sites for long periods. A complete cycle must accommodate adsorption, bond formation and breaking, and product desorption.

Energetically, lowering only an intermediate minimum can slow the following reaction. If an intermediate falls from −0.2-0.2−0.2 to −1.2 eV-1.2\,\mathrm{eV}−1.2eV while the next TS remains at 0 eV0\,\mathrm{eV}0eV, the local barrier increases from 0.20.20.2 to 1.2 eV1.2\,\mathrm{eV}1.2eV. A catalyst must be assessed using the height of each subsequent TS above its preceding intermediate, rather than by seeking ever more negative adsorption energies.

6. Au20/CeO2\mathrm{Au}_{20}/\mathrm{CeO}_2Au20​/CeO2​: Active sites can form during the reaction

On a ceria-supported gold cluster, CO can pull a low-coordination Au atom into a mobile Au–CO unit, bringing CO close to lattice oxygen. Ceria supplies oxygen, the Au atom leaves and returns to the cluster, and product desorption helps regenerate the site. This calculated pathway dynamically forms a single-atom active site. Wang et al. (2015)

CO helps Au leave the cluster and react with lattice oxygen. After Au returns, gas-phase oxygen replenishes the vacancy and regenerates the site.

The cycle begins with CO binding to Au at the cluster edge. The Au–CO unit leaves the edge and moves toward the support. CO then attacks lattice oxygen, forming a bent carbon–oxygen intermediate. Desorption of the first CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ molecule leaves an oxygen vacancy in the support, where Au temporarily resides.

Au then returns to the cluster, exposing the oxygen vacancy again. A second CO forms a new Au–CO unit, while O2\mathrm O_2O2​ adsorbs at the vacancy and forms a peroxo species. After the second CO is oxidized, Au returns to the cluster and the remaining O fills the lattice vacancy. The support supplies lattice oxygen and is subsequently replenished by gas-phase oxygen, the defining feature of a Mars–van Krevelen mechanism.

The mobile Au–CO site facilitates product release: desorbing the first CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ molecule costs 0.27 eV0.27\,\mathrm{eV}0.27eV, compared with 1.29 eV1.29\,\mathrm{eV}1.29eV for the corresponding path reacting at a cluster site. The barrier for Au to return from the oxygen vacancy to the cluster is 0.89 eV0.89\,\mathrm{eV}0.89eV, making this the rate-limiting step of the calculated path. A desorption energy difference and a barrier to crossing a TS describe distinct processes. Wang et al. (2015)

Catalyst regeneration means restoring a usable site after a complete cycle. Atomic migration, coordination changes, and electron transfer can all be part of that cycle.

7. Saddle points and reaction energies on a potential energy surface

A minimum energy path (MEP) connects the relevant local minima. Perpendicular to the path, the energy has been locally minimized; along the path, it can still rise or fall. An arbitrary connecting curve may pass over higher slopes, so the chosen path directly affects the barrier.

The forward barrier, reaction energy, and reverse barrier are:

Eafwd=ETS−EIS,ΔE=EFS−EIS,E_a^{\mathrm{fwd}}=E_{\mathrm{TS}}-E_{\mathrm{IS}}, \qquad \Delta E=E_{\mathrm{FS}}-E_{\mathrm{IS}}, Eafwd​=ETS​−EIS​,ΔE=EFS​−EIS​,

Earev=ETS−EFS=Eafwd−ΔE.E_a^{\mathrm{rev}} =E_{\mathrm{TS}}-E_{\mathrm{FS}} =E_a^{\mathrm{fwd}}-\Delta E. Earev​=ETS​−EFS​=Eafwd​−ΔE.

An exothermic reaction satisfies ΔE<0\Delta E<0ΔE<0, so the reverse barrier through the same saddle point is higher. Adding the same constant to all energies leaves these differences unchanged. For example, with EIS=−10.0E_{\mathrm{IS}}=-10.0EIS​=−10.0, ETS=−9.4E_{\mathrm{TS}}=-9.4ETS​=−9.4, and EFS=−10.8 eVE_{\mathrm{FS}}=-10.8\,\mathrm{eV}EFS​=−10.8eV, the forward barrier is 0.6 eV0.6\,\mathrm{eV}0.6eV, the reaction energy is −0.8 eV-0.8\,\mathrm{eV}−0.8eV, and the reverse barrier is 1.4 eV1.4\,\mathrm{eV}1.4eV.

A TS is a first-order saddle point. It first satisfies the stationarity condition in all relevant coordinates:

∇E(RTS)=0.\nabla E(\mathbf R_{\mathrm{TS}})=0. ∇E(RTS​)=0.

The Hessian matrix then describes the local curvature:

Hab=∂2E∂Ra∂Rb.H_{ab}=\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial R_a\partial R_b}. Hab​=∂Ra​∂Rb​∂2E​.

The curvature is negative along one internal direction and positive along the others. One negative eigenvalue of the mass-weighted Hessian corresponds to an imaginary frequency, whose mode should follow the intended reaction direction. Translational, rotational, and other zero modes are treated separately. Descending in both directions along the unstable mode tests whether the saddle connects the intended reactant and product.

8. Constrained scans and gold clusters supported on thin MgO

Fixing one reaction coordinate

Constrained energy minimization is useful when the main geometric change is clear. For example, progressively shorten a forming C–O bond while relaxing the other coordinates that are allowed to move.

Start from the optimized initial state, fix the reaction coordinate qqq, and perform electronic self-consistency and constrained structural optimization. Then change qqq by a small amount and use the preceding structure as the next initial guess. This produces a relaxed energy scan:

Erel(q)=min⁡R: Q(R)=qE(R).E_{\mathrm{rel}}(q) =\min_{\mathbf R:\,Q(\mathbf R)=q}E(\mathbf R). Erel​(q)=R:Q(R)=qmin​E(R).

Q(R)Q(\mathbf R)Q(R) extracts the selected coordinate from the full atomic configuration. In practice, the optimization generally finds a local minimum on the constraint surface. Using the initial state qaq_aqa​ as the reference:

ΔE(q)=Erel(q)−Erel(qa).\Delta E(q)=E_{\mathrm{rel}}(q)-E_{\mathrm{rel}}(q_a). ΔE(q)=Erel​(q)−Erel​(qa​).

Check structural continuity during the scan and use smaller steps near the maximum. If the reaction involves substantial rotation, sideways motion, or several bonds changing together, add coordinates or optimize the whole path. Forward and reverse scans can also help identify different branches of local structures.

The scan maximum is an initial guess for the TS. Refine the stationary point in all relevant degrees of freedom, check for one reaction-related imaginary frequency, and descend along both directions of that mode to establish whether the constrained-path maximum is a true transition state.

Why Au20\mathrm{Au}_{20}Au20​/MgO/Mo has a low barrier

The Mo substrate supplies electrons through two thin MgO layers to the two-dimensional Au20\mathrm{Au}_{20}Au20​ interface. These electrons enter the 2π∗2\pi^*2π∗ antibonding states of adsorbed oxygen and lengthen O–O. CO on a neighboring MgO site can then react with it over a low barrier. The gold-cluster interface anchors and activates oxygen, while the MgO site allows CO to approach from a suitable direction. Zhang, Yoon & Landman (2007)

Mo supplies electrons through thin MgO to the gold-cluster interface. As the C–O distance decreases, the system crosses a maximum of approximately 0.15 eV0.15\,\mathrm{eV}0.15eV and forms carbon dioxide.

This LH path starts from configuration aaa, in which CO and oxygen are coadsorbed. The scan coordinate is the distance from the C atom in CO to the nearest O atom in the oxygen molecule:

q=d(C,O(2)).q=d(\mathrm C,\mathrm O^{(2)}). q=d(C,O(2)).

The C–O distance starts at 2.85 A˚2.85\,\text{\AA}2.85A˚ in the initial state. In configuration bbb near the maximum, it has shortened to 1.60 A˚1.60\,\text{\AA}1.60A˚, while O–O has lengthened from 1.521.521.52 to 1.55 A˚1.55\,\text{\AA}1.55A˚. After the new C–O bond forms, CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ leaves the surface. Relative to the coadsorbed initial state, the barrier along this path is approximately:

E‡=E(b)−E(a)≃0.15 eV.E^\ddagger=E(b)-E(a)\simeq0.15\,\mathrm{eV}. E‡=E(b)−E(a)≃0.15eV.

If the horizontal axis is the C–O distance itself, the reaction proceeds toward decreasing distance. The peak height measures the barrier, while the subsequent energy decrease represents the energy released in product formation.

The adsorption site of CO changes the path. CO adsorbed at the Au edge gives a barrier of approximately 1.0 eV1.0\,\mathrm{eV}1.0eV; an ER path in which gas-phase CO directly attacks adsorbed oxygen has a barrier of approximately 0.2 eV0.2\,\mathrm{eV}0.2eV. The low barrier combines electronic and geometric effects: oxygen first gains antibonding electrons, and CO then approaches the activated oxygen from a neighboring MgO site. Zhang, Yoon & Landman (2007), Supporting Information

9. Self-tests

Why can a reaction be slow even when its products have much lower energy?

Reaction energy compares the initial and final states; the rate depends on the local barrier from the current minimum to the TS. Stabilizing products and lowering the transition state are different changes.

How can you assess whether a catalyst can sustain repeated turnover?

It must activate reactants and lower key barriers, but also convert residual intermediates, release products, and regenerate sites. Strong adsorption alone does not guarantee a high turnover rate.

VI. Nudged Elastic Band Method

1. From one reaction coordinate to a chain of configurations

A single bond length describes some reactions clearly, but molecular rotation, concerted changes in several bonds, or surface reconstruction often require more coordinates. NEB (nudged elastic band) starts from known initial and final states and directly optimizes a chain of complete configurations, allowing the whole chain to bend toward a low-energy channel.

The endpoints lie in two energy minima. The initial path must adjust in configuration space to pass through the low-energy channel connecting them.

A configuration of NNN atoms is written as:

R=(x1,y1,z1,…,xN,yN,zN),E=E(R).\mathbf R=(x_1,y_1,z_1,\ldots,x_N,y_N,z_N), \qquad E=E(\mathbf R). R=(x1​,y1​,z1​,…,xN​,yN​,zN​),E=E(R).

An image consists of the complete atomic coordinates and the corresponding potential energy and forces. A two-dimensional contour plot is only a schematic of the high-dimensional potential energy surface (PES): each point represents the entire atomic system. Fixing some substrate atoms reduces the number of degrees of freedom that can be optimized.

Each iteration first solves the electronic problem at the corresponding geometry. Magnetic systems also require tracking the electronic spin state and using consistent spin treatment across all images. The nuclear path is optimized on the selected electronic potential energy surface; transitions between different spin surfaces require a nonadiabatic treatment.

Discretize the path as:

R0,R1,…,RM−1,RM.\mathbf R_0,\mathbf R_1,\ldots,\mathbf R_{M-1},\mathbf R_M. R0​,R1​,…,RM−1​,RM​.

There are M+1M+1M+1 images. R0\mathbf R_0R0​ and RM\mathbf R_MRM​ are the optimized IS and FS and are usually fixed, while the intermediate images are optimized together. The distances between neighboring configurations are:

di+=∣Ri+1−Ri∣,di−=∣Ri−Ri−1∣.d_i^+=|\mathbf R_{i+1}-\mathbf R_i|, \qquad d_i^-=|\mathbf R_i-\mathbf R_{i-1}|. di+​=∣Ri+1​−Ri​∣,di−​=∣Ri​−Ri−1​∣.

With a Cartesian metric, square and sum all displacement components of corresponding atoms, then take the square root. All images must therefore share consistent atom counts, element ordering, atom correspondence, and cell descriptions.

More images resolve curved paths, intermediate minima, and variations near the maximum, at the cost of more electronic-structure calculations. Usually, first establish a clear channel, then increase sampling where the path changes rapidly. The energies can be plotted against cumulative configuration-space distance after optimization; this measures reaction progress, not elapsed time.

2. Why NEB projects the forces

If each intermediate configuration is minimized independently, the images fall into energy minima and leave the barrier region unsampled. Ordinary connecting springs can instead straighten a curved path to shorten the band, causing corner cutting. NEB separates the two tasks: the physical force moves the path perpendicular to its tangent toward the valley, while the spring force distributes images along the path.

Tangential and perpendicular components of the physical force

The physical force on image iii is:

Fiphys=−∇E(Ri).\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}}=-\nabla E(\mathbf R_i). Fiphys​=−∇E(Ri​).

Let τi\boldsymbol\tau_iτi​ be a unit tangent estimated from neighboring configurations, satisfying τi⋅τi=1\boldsymbol\tau_i\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i=1τi​⋅τi​=1. The projection of the physical force along the path is:

Fi,∥phys=(Fiphys⋅τi)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{phys}} =(\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,∥phys​=(Fiphys​⋅τi​)τi​.

The dot product gives the scalar tangential component. Multiplying by the unit tangent gives its vector projection. Subtracting this projection leaves the perpendicular component:

Fi,⊥phys=Fiphys−(Fiphys⋅τi)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\perp}^{\mathrm{phys}} =\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}} -(\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,⊥phys​=Fiphys​−(Fiphys​⋅τi​)τi​.

It satisfies Fi,⊥phys⋅τi=0\mathbf F_{i,\perp}^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_i=0Fi,⊥phys​⋅τi​=0. Normalize the tangent before applying these formulas directly.

The physical tangential force would push images toward the energy minima, so ordinary NEB removes it. The retained perpendicular force lets the path move down the valley walls toward the MEP. A converged MEP satisfies:

F⊥phys=0.\mathbf F_\perp^{\mathrm{phys}}=\mathbf 0. F⊥phys​=0.

A tangential downhill force can still exist along the MEP. The complete physical force vanishes only at the TS or another stationary point.

Retaining only the tangential spring force

With a uniform spring constant kkk, the tangential spring force is:

Fi,∥spring=k(di+−di−)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{spring}} =k(d_i^+-d_i^-)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,∥spring​=k(di+​−di−​)τi​.

When the forward spacing is larger, the spring pulls the image along +τi+\boldsymbol\tau_i+τi​. Tangential balance makes the forward and backward spacings equal. The perpendicular spring component is removed so that it does not straighten a curved channel.

The effective force used for optimization is therefore:

FiNEB=Fi,⊥phys+Fi,∥spring.\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{NEB}} =\mathbf F_{i,\perp}^{\mathrm{phys}} +\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{spring}}. FiNEB​=Fi,⊥phys​+Fi,∥spring​.

kkk can be expressed in eV A˚−2\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}eVA˚−2. Multiplying by a configuration-space distance gives force units of eV A˚−1\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-1}eVA˚−1.

For example, take τ=(1,0)\boldsymbol\tau=(1,0)τ=(1,0) and Fphys=(2,−3) eV A˚−1\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}=(2,-3)\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-1}Fphys=(2,−3)eVA˚−1, forward and backward spacings of 222 and 1 A˚1\,\text{\AA}1A˚, and k=1.5 eV A˚−2k=1.5\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}k=1.5eVA˚−2. The perpendicular physical force is (0,−3)(0,-3)(0,−3) and the spring force is (1.5,0)(1.5,0)(1.5,0), giving:

FNEB=(1.5,−3) eV A˚−1.\mathbf F^{\mathrm{NEB}}=(1.5,-3)\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-1}. FNEB=(1.5,−3)eVA˚−1.

FiNEB=0\mathbf F_i^{\mathrm{NEB}}=0FiNEB​=0 means that the perpendicular physical force vanishes and the tangential spring forces balance. The removed physical tangential force can remain nonzero, so an ordinary converged image can lie on a slope of the MEP.

3. Variable spring constants: denser sampling at high energy

Accurate peak energies require denser sampling near the saddle point. Increasing the spring constants in high-energy regions concentrates the available images in these segments.

Let kik_iki​ connect images i−1i-1i−1 and iii, and define:

Eref=max⁡(EIS,EFS),E~i=max⁡(Ei−1,Ei),E_{\mathrm{ref}}=\max(E_{\mathrm{IS}},E_{\mathrm{FS}}), \qquad \widetilde E_i=\max(E_{i-1},E_i), Eref​=max(EIS​,EFS​),Ei​=max(Ei−1​,Ei​),

Δk=kmax⁡−kmin⁡.\Delta k=k_{\max}-k_{\min}. Δk=kmax​−kmin​.

Emax⁡E_{\max}Emax​ is the highest physical energy on the current band. Assign each segment's spring constant using the higher energy of its two endpoints:

ki={kmax⁡−Δk Emax⁡−E~iEmax⁡−Eref,E~i>Eref,kmin⁡,E~i≤Eref.k_i= \begin{cases} k_{\max}-\Delta k\,\dfrac{E_{\max}-\widetilde E_i}{E_{\max}-E_{\mathrm{ref}}}, &\widetilde E_i>E_{\mathrm{ref}},\\[6pt] k_{\min},&\widetilde E_i\leq E_{\mathrm{ref}}. \end{cases} ki​=⎩⎪⎪⎨⎪⎪⎧​kmax​−ΔkEmax​−Eref​Emax​−Ei​​,kmin​,​Ei​>Eref​,Ei​≤Eref​.​

When E~i=Emax⁡\widetilde E_i=E_{\max}Ei​=Emax​, the segment uses the stiffest spring, kmax⁡k_{\max}kmax​. As its energy decreases to ErefE_{\mathrm{ref}}Eref​, the constant returns continuously to kmin⁡k_{\min}kmin​. If Emax⁡=ErefE_{\max}=E_{\mathrm{ref}}Emax​=Eref​, use constant springs to avoid a zero denominator.

When the forward and backward spring constants differ, the tangential force is:

Fi,∥spring=(ki+1di+−kidi−)τi.\mathbf F_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{spring}} =(k_{i+1}d_i^+-k_i d_i^-)\boldsymbol\tau_i. Fi,∥spring​=(ki+1​di+​−ki​di−​)τi​.

Tangential equilibrium requires equal tensions on the two sides:

ki+1di+≈kidi−.k_{i+1}d_i^+\approx k_i d_i^-. ki+1​di+​≈ki​di−​.

At the same tension, a larger kkk gives a smaller spacing, so more images gather in high-energy regions. These springs control numerical sampling; they leave the physical potential energy unchanged.

For example, with Eref=0E_{\mathrm{ref}}=0Eref​=0, Emax⁡=0.8 eVE_{\max}=0.8\,\mathrm{eV}Emax​=0.8eV, kmin⁡=1k_{\min}=1kmin​=1, and kmax⁡=5 eV A˚−2k_{\max}=5\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}kmax​=5eVA˚−2, a segment at E~i=0.6 eV\widetilde E_i=0.6\,\mathrm{eV}Ei​=0.6eV has:

ki=5−40.8−0.60.8=4 eV A˚−2.k_i=5-4\frac{0.8-0.6}{0.8} =4\,\mathrm{eV}\,\text{\AA}^{-2}. ki​=5−40.80.8−0.6​=4eVA˚−2.

4. Climbing Image NEB: moving directly toward a saddle point

The highest sampled image in ordinary NEB may lie on one side of the maximum. CI-NEB selects an image and drives it uphill along the path and downhill perpendicular to the path, directly toward the saddle point.

The physical force decomposes as F⊥+F∥\mathbf F_\perp+\mathbf F_\parallelF⊥​+F∥​. Retaining the perpendicular component and reversing the tangential component gives the target force F⊥−F∥\mathbf F_\perp-\mathbf F_\parallelF⊥​−F∥​. This is equivalent to subtracting twice the tangential component from the physical force:

FCI=Fphys−2(Fphys⋅τ)τ.\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}} =\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}} -2(\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau)\boldsymbol\tau. FCI=Fphys−2(Fphys⋅τ)τ.

Substituting Fphys=−∇E\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}=-\nabla EFphys=−∇E gives:

FCI=−∇E+2(∇E⋅τ)τ.\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}} =-\nabla E+2(\nabla E\cdot\boldsymbol\tau)\boldsymbol\tau. FCI=−∇E+2(∇E⋅τ)τ.

First obtain a reasonable channel with ordinary NEB. Then select the highest-energy intermediate image as the climbing image and remove its spring force. It can then reach the maximum without being constrained by equal spacing. The other images continue to use ordinary NEB forces and provide the path shape and local tangent.

Using the same example with τ=(1,0)\boldsymbol\tau=(1,0)τ=(1,0) and Fphys=(2,−3)\mathbf F^{\mathrm{phys}}=(2,-3)Fphys=(2,−3):

FCI=(2,−3)−2(2,0)=(−2,−3).\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}} =(2,-3)-2(2,0)=(-2,-3). FCI=(2,−3)−2(2,0)=(−2,−3).

The tangential component reverses sign, the perpendicular component stays unchanged, and no spring force is added.

The tangential and perpendicular directions are orthogonal, so FCI=0\mathbf F^{\mathrm{CI}}=0FCI=0 requires both components of the physical force to vanish, giving a physical stationary point. Check for one reaction-related negative-curvature mode and verify the initial and final states reached by descending in both directions along that mode to identify the intended TS.

Barrier accuracy has two aspects: whether the path has found the intended channel, and whether sampling near the maximum is sufficient. Different initial guesses for competing mechanisms address the first; more images and CI refinement address the second.

5. Constructing and optimizing the initial path

The simplest initial path is generated by linear interpolation:

Ri(0)=(1−iM)RIS+iMRFS,i=0,…,M.\mathbf R_i^{(0)} =\left(1-\frac{i}{M}\right)\mathbf R_{\mathrm{IS}} +\frac{i}{M}\mathbf R_{\mathrm{FS}}, \qquad i=0,\ldots,M. Ri(0)​=(1−Mi​)RIS​+Mi​RFS​,i=0,…,M.

Every coordinate is interpolated with weight i/Mi/Mi/M, so the initial images are equally spaced in Cartesian configuration space. Their energy spacing depends on the potential energy surface. The endpoints should use consistent cells, atom numbering, constraints, electronic states, and computational accuracy.

For an atom moving from (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) to (2,1) A˚(2,1)\,\text{\AA}(2,1)A˚ with five images in total, M=4M=4M=4. The three internal initial guesses are (0.5,0.25)(0.5,0.25)(0.5,0.25), (1,0.5)(1,0.5)(1,0.5), and (1.5,0.75) A˚(1.5,0.75)\,\text{\AA}(1.5,0.75)A˚. A many-atom system interpolates all coordinates simultaneously.

Inspect each interpolated geometry. Linear interpolation can make two exchanging atoms coincide, or compress internal bonds when a molecule rotates substantially. Add physically reasonable intermediate configurations or interpolate in segments when needed. With periodic boundaries, first unwrap coordinates onto a continuous branch consistent with the intended hop, then generate the path.

The NEB optimization proceeds as follows:

  1. Calculate the electronic energy and physical atomic forces for each image.
  2. Estimate and normalize the tangent from neighboring configurations.
  3. Combine the perpendicular physical force with the tangential spring force and update the intermediate configurations.
  4. Once the path is stable, activate the climbing image and refine the saddle point.
  5. Check electronic self-consistency, converged forces, structural continuity, and sampling near the maximum. Extract the barrier from the energy difference between the relevant IS and TS.

6. Surface diffusion as a path-search problem

Chemical reactions connect structures with different bonding, while surface diffusion connects different adsorption positions. Both are transitions between minima on a potential energy surface, so both can be studied with NEB.

Diffusion may involve molecular rotation, coordination changes, and surface relaxation. The energy difference from the starting adsorption site to the CI-NEB saddle point is the barrier for that hop. A simple hopping model is:

Γ=νexp⁡ ⁣(−EdiffkBT).\Gamma=\nu\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{\mathrm{diff}}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right). Γ=νexp(−kB​TEdiff​​).

Γ\GammaΓ is the hopping rate, ν\nuν the attempt frequency, and EdiffE_{\mathrm{diff}}Ediff​ the diffusion barrier. If the endpoints have different energies, the reverse barrier through the same saddle satisfies:

Earev=Eafwd−ΔE.E_a^{\mathrm{rev}}=E_a^{\mathrm{fwd}}-\Delta E. Earev​=Eafwd​−ΔE.

A deeper adsorption site requires more energy to escape. Equal endpoint energies imply equal forward and reverse barriers, but a high maximum can still lie between them. Obtaining a macroscopic diffusion coefficient from a single-hop rate also requires the hop distance, spatial dimension, accessible neighbors, and correlations between hops.

7. Graphene/Ru: from substrate defects to two-step CO oxidation

Local defects in the Ru surface weaken bonding between Ru and the carbon atoms above them, making those carbon atoms more able to donate electrons to adsorbed oxygen. Occupation of oxygen antibonding states lengthens O–O. Oxygen then reacts with gas-phase CO over relatively low barriers to form carbon dioxide. Guo, Yam & Zhang (2018)

Two substrate defects are considered: IA denotes a substitutional impurity atom replacing a surface Ru atom, and V denotes a single vacancy in the surface Ru layer. The active region lies in the graphene directly above the defect, where oxygen adsorbs on carbon atoms.

IA and V denote two substrate-defect types. The two energy profiles below describe consecutive oxidation steps in the same Au-substitution model, with barriers of 0.540.540.54 and 0.48 eV0.48\,\mathrm{eV}0.48eV.

The specific two-step reaction uses the same Au-substituted Ru(0001) model, with graphene in the fcc-top registry. Au weakens nearby C–Ru bonding; upon oxygen adsorption, electrons enter the oxygen 2π∗2\pi^*2π∗ antibonding states. Oxygen gains approximately 0.99∣e∣0.99|e|0.99∣e∣, O–O lengthens from 1.231.231.23 to 1.48 A˚1.48\,\text{\AA}1.48A˚, and the adsorption energy is −0.43 eV-0.43\,\mathrm{eV}−0.43eV.

Gas-phase CO reacts with adsorbed oxygen through an Eley–Rideal (ER) mechanism. Near the first TS, O–O stretches while a new C–O bond forms. The first CO2\mathrm{CO}_2CO2​ molecule is released, leaving one adsorbed oxygen atom:

COgas+O2,ads⟶CO2+Oads,Ea,1=0.54 eV.\mathrm{CO}_{\mathrm{gas}}+\mathrm O_{2,\mathrm{ads}} \longrightarrow\mathrm{CO}_2+\mathrm O_{\mathrm{ads}}, \qquad E_{a,1}=0.54\,\mathrm{eV}. COgas​+O2,ads​⟶CO2​+Oads​,Ea,1​=0.54eV.

A second CO removes the remaining oxygen, forming another carbon dioxide molecule:

COgas+Oads⟶CO2,Ea,2=0.48 eV.\mathrm{CO}_{\mathrm{gas}}+\mathrm O_{\mathrm{ads}} \longrightarrow\mathrm{CO}_2, \qquad E_{a,2}=0.48\,\mathrm{eV}. COgas​+Oads​⟶CO2​,Ea,2​=0.48eV.

These barriers belong to consecutive steps in the same Au system, each measured from its own initial state to its CI-NEB saddle point. After the second step, the graphene site can accept another oxygen molecule and begin the next cycle. Guo, Yam & Zhang (2018)

The rate constant of each step can be understood using a thermally activated form:

ki≃Aiexp⁡ ⁣(−Ea,ikBT).k_i\simeq A_i\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_{a,i}}{k_{\mathrm B}T}\right). ki​≃Ai​exp(−kB​TEa,i​​).

The first step requires adsorbed oxygen molecules, whereas the second requires the remaining oxygen atoms. Their coverages depend on adsorption and the preceding reactions. Identifying the rate-determining step therefore requires both the local rate constants and these surface populations. Electron transfer explains oxygen activation, CI-NEB describes barrier crossing, and the complete cycle explains sustained site turnover.

8. Self-tests

Does zero ordinary NEB force imply zero physical atomic force?

Ordinary NEB requires only a vanishing perpendicular physical force and balanced tangential spring forces; a physical tangential force may remain. The climbing image reverses the physical tangential force, so its effective force vanishes only when both tangential and perpendicular physical forces vanish.

Why do variable springs increase the density of images at high energy?

At equilibrium, neighboring springs have equal tension. High-energy regions use larger spring constants, giving smaller spacings at the same tension and therefore denser sampling.
